title: 3 up, 3 down Preseason Week 1: Struggles on offense and defense
summary: The Atlanta Falcons registered their first unofficial game of the 2026 season, when they opened the Mercedes Benz Stadium up for a matchup against last year’s AFC Finalist Denver Broncos. Despite Michael Penix still not being cleared for full contact and Bijan Robinson also being held out, there was real excitement as new head coach […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - AUGUST 14: Tua Tagovailoa #1 of the Atlanta Falcons recovers his own fumble against the Denver Broncos during the first quarter of a NFL preseason game at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on August 14, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Kevin C. Cox/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Atlanta Falcons registered their first unofficial game of the 2026 season, when they opened the Mercedes Benz Stadium up for a matchup against last year’s AFC Finalist Denver Broncos. Despite Michael Penix still not being cleared for full contact and Bijan Robinson also being held out, there was real excitement as new head coach Kevin Stefanski announced that the starters would play in the preseason in Atlanta for the first time in years. That excitement was quickly dashed, however, as the Falcons found themselves down 24-0 at halftime, before mercifully going down with a whimper to the tune of a final scoreline of 27-7. This night showed that there was a lot of work still to do, with the regular season about a month away from kicking off. This is a look at whose stock is pointing up after the first preseason game and whose is pointing down. Up Jack Strand Jack Strand is looking to achieve the rare feat of becoming an undrafted rookie quarterback to make a 53-man NFL roster to start the season, and he looked by far the best quarterback that the Falcons deployed in this game. In fairness, it didn’t take much to look better than Cooper Rush or Tua Tagovailoa (we’ll get to them), but Strand looked like he belonged. The numbers won’t stick out at you — the Minnesota State-Moorhead alum went 6/12 with 50 yards and no touchdowns through the air — but the most impressive throws of the night from an Atlanta signal caller were a couple of his incompletions. The first was a deep shot with perfect placement to Vinny Anthony against double coverage which would have been an incredibly thrown 38-yard touchdown had Anthony not slowed down at the end of the play. The next was a laster beam thrown in the direction of Kristian Wilkerson, who looked behind the defense and poised for a 56-yard touchdown before Sean Fresch made an incredible leaping play to get a hand on it. If those get completed, we’re talking about an elite preseason debut performance. Strand exhibited NFL level arm talent when he was allowed to rip it, and he utilized his big body multiple times to successfully convert short yardage QB sneaks, including one from a yard out which represented Atlanta’s only score of the night. Tyler Goodson Tis the season of position battles all up and down the roster and, much like last year, the battle for that third running back spot on the depth chart is going to be a competitive one. Tyler Goodson, a former Georgia High School player of the year out of North Gwinnett, dealt the first real blow in that competition against incumbent Nathan Carter and new addition Trey Sermon. Goodson was the best runner of the night for the Falcons, and was the only player out of the eight to take at least one carry (including the quarterbacks) to generate a higher yards per attempt mark than 3.0. In fact, he averaged a full yard more per attempt than the next best Falcon (4.0). The former Indianapolis Colt looked spry kicking it to the left for the game long rush of eight yards for the Falcons on a night where everybody else looked stuck in the mud. Nothing demonstrated how differently the nights of Carter (6 carries, 8 rushing yards) and Goodson went than a sequence in the third quarter where the Falcons had the ball on Denver’s 5-yard line and gave each of them an opportunity. Carter was stuffed and went backward for a 1-yard loss. Goodson took the subsequent handoff and was stonewalled for what looked like a minimal gain, before he kept his legs churning to turn it into a very impressive 5-yard run to the 1-yard line, setting up Strand’s sneak touchdown. Special Teams If there’s one thing the Falcons can truly hang their hat on from this blowout loss, it was their play on special teams, which is not nothing given how poorly that unit played throughout the two year Raheem Morris regime. Nick Folk didn’t get much work in, kicking in his only extra point of the night (no attempted field goals), but the kickoff and punt coverage was a thing of beauty. Jake Bailey and Matthew Hayball combined to punt the ball eight times (four opportunities each), for 376 combined yards, and the Falcons’ gunners ran down the Broncos to the tune of five punts downed inside the 20 and four returned for just 13 meager yards. Denver did not have much more luck in their kickoff returns either, generating returns of just 22 and 21 yards. While nobody broke any big gains on kickoff returns on Atlanta’s side, either, they did beat Denver out with an average of 28.8 yards per return versus 21.5 on the other side. Denver’s average starting field position off kickoffs was the 23-yard line, while Atlanta’s was the 32.5-yard line. Down The entire first team defense I know and understand that the first team defense the Falcons deployed in this game was not complete, particularly as they were missing Jessie Bates Xavier Watts and Divine Deablo while voluntarily relegating James Pearce Jr. to the second team following announcement of his 8-game suspension . They were, however, also facing a Broncos offense down their starting quarterback, their starting running back, their top wide receiver and down to their fourth string center. In the battle of banged up first teams, the Broncos absolutely cooked the Falcons’ defense, cutting through it like a cold knife through warm butter on a 7-play opening drive where presumed starting cornerback Mike Hughes gave up two explosive plays, including the crucial 40-yard reception to Courtland Sutton which set up an opening drive touchdown. The biggest concern for the Falcons was just how little resistance they had rushing four, as Jarrett Stidham had all day in the pocket any time he dropped back when the Falcons did not send a blitz. To win in this league, you have to be able to successfully rush the passer without the extra men sent at least some of the time and right now the Falcons’ defense seems miles away from that. They also allowed multiple explosive runs and looked like a unit wholly unprepared for the very quickly approaching regular season. “Next Man Up” Tackles – Michael Jerrell and Ethan Onianwa The Falcons were down starting right tackle Jawaan Taylor in this game as he spent some time on the PUP list during camp and is still working back into game shape, and they at one point lost starting left tackle Jake Matthews. As a result, they had the opportunity to more closely evaluate both Michael Jerrell and Ethan Onianwa, who have been dominating first team reps in camp due to Taylor and presumed backup right tackle Wanya Morris’ absences. Both of those players failed the first preseason evaluation spectacularly. Jerrell, who was given the first look at RT before sliding for an extended period to LT after Matthews left the game, was beaten frequently as a primary catalyst for why the first team offense looked stuck in mud during their couple of drives. Jerrell, however, we have seen extensively in the past as the guy who failed to beat out Elijah Wilkinson for last year’s RT position after Kaleb McGary’s season ending injury. Ethan Onianwa, being a rookie, is someone we had not seen yet beyond the controlled environment of training camp, and he could not have given off a worse first impression. Jonathan Cooper at one point so decisively beat him off the edge that Tagovailoa did not even have the time to throw what looked like set up screen pass. Later, he gave up the pressure and hit on Cooper Rush which directly resulted in an interception, before giving up a third down pressure later in the second quarter to kill another drive. The Falcons had better hope that Jawaan Taylor is good to go for Week 1 and that Wanya Morris is healthy and good enough to be the team’s swing tackle for…

title: Falcons DE James Pearce Jr. will serve 8-game suspension in regular NFL season
summary: We finally know what James Pearce Jr.’s suspension will look like after he was charged with a variety of felonies connected to alleged stalking and threats against his former partner, WNBA star Rickea Jackson. The league minimum suspension for violence against women and children was set several years ago, post-Ray Rice. to six games. The […]
full_text: Dec 21, 2025; Glendale, Arizona, USA; Atlanta Falcons linebacker James Pearce Jr. (27) against the Arizona Cardinals at State Farm Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Mark J. Rebilas-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect We finally know what James Pearce Jr.’s suspension will look like after he was charged with a variety of felonies connected to alleged stalking and threats against his former partner, WNBA star Rickea Jackson . The league minimum suspension for violence against women and children was set several years ago, post-Ray Rice. to six games. The NFL has issued Pearce an eight-game suspension. Pearce is free to participate in the remainder of training camp and the preseason. Prior to the regular season, he will be moved to the commissioner’s exempt list, opening up a roster spot for those eight weeks. Pearce was able to plea down his charges and must complete a diversion program in lieu of other consequences. I am unaware of the specifics of Pearce’s program or Florida’s process, but in Georgia the program often includes the completion of a treatment program and counseling and community service as basic elements. When a player is suspended, they forfeit game checks for each week they aren’t permitted to play, and they are not permitted to be at the facility or around their coaches and teammates. For Pearce, it goes a bit further. According to Spotrac, Pearce’s remaining guaranteed money is no longer guaranteed, and the Falcons can recoup nearly a million of Pearce Jr’s $8.8m signing bonus. Sometimes it takes hitting someone in the wallet to make them learn a hard lesson, and Pearce Jr’s wallet is being hit HARD. James Pearce Jr.'s 8-game suspension from the #Falcons will cost him $446,664 in base salary. Atlanta can also recoup $982,528 of signing bonus per the conduct violation. Additionally, the guarantee on the remaining $6.65M through 2028 is now voided. — Spotrac (@spotrac) August 14, 2026 Everyone deserves the chance to learn and grow from their mistakes, including JPJ. Honestly, between the diversion program and the eight games, he’s still getting off light considering how horrifying the accusations and the confirmed instances of harassment and stalking are. I truly hope he takes this opportunity and his time away from the game to work on becoming a better version of himself.

title: Falcons – Broncos preseason recap: Not for the faint of heart
summary: Well, that was not fun. Preseason games are fertile ground for overreactions, and we’ll definitely see in the weeks ahead that we were too excited about some things (Jack Strand? Malcolm DeWalt IV?) and too down on others (Tua Tagovailoa? Mike Hughes?). There are small sample sizes, vanilla game plans, and matchups we’ll never see […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - AUGUST 14: Courtland Sutton #14 of the Denver Broncos pulls in this reception against Mike Hughes #21 of the Atlanta Falcons in the first quarter at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on August 14, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Kevin C. Cox/Getty Images) | Getty Images Well, that was not fun. Preseason games are fertile ground for overreactions, and we’ll definitely see in the weeks ahead that we were too excited about some things (Jack Strand? Malcolm DeWalt IV?) and too down on others (Tua Tagovailoa? Mike Hughes?). There are small sample sizes, vanilla game plans, and matchups we’ll never see in the regular season to consider. And despite all that, the broad contours can feel awfully truthful. The Atlanta Falcons have to earn the trust of this fanbase after eight straight losing seasons and a lot of “this is going to be great oh no it’s on fire” stretches over that span. Fighting the urge to declare this team the same old, same old is tough in light of history and what we saw Friday night. Because what we saw Friday night was ugly. The Falcons lost 27-7. They had a couple of serious drives, one which ended with a Jack Strand touchdown plunge and the other which ended in a tipped Cooper Rush pass that was returned 98 yards for a Denver score. They looked like a much lesser team compared to the Broncos, who are an AFC Super Bowl hopeful in 2026. Whatever string these players are on the depth charts for either team, the Broncos players just seem bigger/faster/stronger. Breaking tackles, getting open, winning the LOS. — Joe Patrick (@JoePatrick) August 14, 2026 How much stock should we put in that? On one hand, without Jawaan Taylor or Jake Matthews or Bijan Robinson, the offense is obviously going to be lesser. On the other, 28 yards on two drives for offensive starters is the kind of result that sees you fall behind by a touchdown or more in a regular season game. Getting burnt to a crisp by Jarrett Stidham is a bad result no matter how many starters are out or how little effort you’re putting into complexity and pressure, and no matter how talented Denver’s offense may be around Stidham. When you’re talking about special teams being far more impressive, you are talking about a team that has not played well, and we all fear that this team is going to get to the regular season and not play well. I think this franchise is too hellbent on digging out of the past to be nonchalant about this result, unlike the past three regimes when preseason went poorly. I have to question whether their drive to get better will translate to better outcomes, because there’s only so much time and so much talent to work this all out before the opener. But I do ultimately have to cite the unpredictability and sheer weirdness of preseason, where the talent levels on the field are wildly uneven and coaches are putting in varying levels of effort in terms of their creative play calling and effort, in saying this result should not cause us to hit the panic button on the 2026 Falcons season. It should, instead, simply make us wary, which is something we already should be given the way this franchise has let us down again and again. Instead of indulging doom, let’s be sober about what went wrong and bright about what went right, even if those scales are wildly unbalanced. On to the full recap. The Good Jack Strand nearly threw an interception, but he followed that up with a zippy deep ball to Vinny Anthony that missed by a little and then led a touchdown drive that featured a couple of nice short passes to Josh Simon and a sneak for a score. On a night where Cooper Rush looked ghastly, Strand simply seeming far more competent than a UDFA quarterback has any right to likely helped him. Someone has to take control of this RB3 battle, and I think Tyler Goodson is well on his way. I saw a player who showed quality hands when called upon, but more than that showed strong burst and balance as a runner, especially on a long rumble where he stiff armed, absorbed a lot of contact, and stayed on his feet. Given his versatility—he can block, he can catch, and he plays special teams—Goodson just needs to keep it going to take the lead in this particular competition. Tua leaned on Kyle Pitts, who looks lean, sure-handed, and ready to go. Watching Pitts reel in his targets early on and make something of them when the rest of the offense was silent is a good sign for his 2026 season. If Tua’s going to look to the middle of the field for a big target who can catch, Pitts is going to rack them up. Vinny Anthony has been a reliable target at training camp, but he caught my attention with his returns in this one. Anthony looked fast and confident and picked up a couple of really nice kick returns, which can only help his chances of sticking around. The fact that Rush and Strand missed him multiple times does not take anything away from his ability as a receiver, which I think is evident. Chris Blair had maybe the single most impressive offensive play of the night, a leaping grab where he took a big hit and barely saw the ball jostled. Blair has been reliable every summer thus far and should, in my opinion, be ticketed for a practice squad spot at worst. Both Kendal Daniels and Harold Perkins Jr. looked like the kind of aggressive, capable linebackers the Falcons sorely need out there. The team trusting Daniels with the green dot is huge for a mid round rookie, but I’ve thought since he was drafted that Daniels has the requisite smarts and physicality to seize a major role on this defense. Perkins, meanwhile, looks like a ball of fire willing and able to fly to the ball no matter what the offense is doing, something that could make him chaotic fun whenever he gets into games in 2026. It’s very early, but the future looks bright for this group. Josh Woods is going to make this team based on his special teams ability, but the better he looks on defense, the better his chances are. I thought his second half performance was once again strong, as he put up a handful of really good tackles and flew to the ball. Darnay Holmes had one coverage lapse by my count, but otherwise looked good playing quite a bit in the first half. He was aggressive getting to the ball and showed quality instincts, qualities he had with the Raiders that were not on display consistently. He’s spent this summer pushing for a roster spot and may well get it. I thought DeMarcco Hellams, who limped off the field but is hopefully okay, delivered a customarily strong summer night with his tackling. He’s a very logical third safety with Sydney Brown (who also had his moments) filling in a hybrid corner/safety role, and I hope he can lock it up. Your special teams contributors hoping to make it based on preseason performances on defense had their moments in this one. JD Bertrand punched out a ball that Jammie Robinson lunged on, giving Atlanta a shot at its first score of the game. Bertrand faces an uphill battle to make this roster while Robinson seems like a strong bet, and plays like that help both. Jake Bailey showed off a nice leg, averaging 50ish yards on his all-too-frequent boots in this one. The veteran punter is replacing Bradley Pinion, who had been reliable for Atlanta over the past few seasons, and looks like he’ll be a good pickup. If the team wants to keep an alternate option around, Matthew Hayball also delivered some impressive punts of his own. Finally but certainly not least, Malcolm DeWalt IV looks like he might turn into something sooner than later. He looked impressive as a gunner on special teams and made one of the best plays of the night on an underthrown Sam Ehlinger deep ball, reading it perfectly and leaping to snatch it away from Denver’s receiver for an interception in the fourth quarter. If you can play special teams at a high level and make plays like that, you have a future in this league, even if the pick was (unfairly, cruelly) overturned. The Ugly The starting offense looked bad. There…

title: Ravens’ rookie pass-catchers dazzle in preseason win over Eagles
summary: Jesse Minter notched his first win as the Baltimore Ravens’ head coach on Saturday night, taking down the Philadelphia Eagles by a score of 24-7. “It was a great experience,” Minter said after the game. “I want to give a ton of credit to our coaching staff.” Offensive coordinator Declan Doyle led his unit to […]
full_text: Aug 15, 2026; Baltimore, Maryland, USA; Baltimore Ravens wide receiver Ja’Kobi Lane (6) is greeted by teammates after his touchdown catch during the second quarter against the Philadelphia Eagles at M&T Bank Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Mitch Stringer-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Jesse Minter notched his first win as the Baltimore Ravens’ head coach on Saturday night, taking down the Philadelphia Eagles by a score of 24-7. “It was a great experience,” Minter said after the game. “I want to give a ton of credit to our coaching staff.” Offensive coordinator Declan Doyle led his unit to 440 yards and 31 first downs, dominating with long drives throughout the game and putting up lopsided time-of-possession and play-count numbers. On the other side of the ball, Minter and defensive coordinator Anthony Weaver oversaw a near-shutout; the Eagles’ only points came with 2:24 left in the game after averaging just 4.0 yards per play and going 0-for-9 on third down. Special teams was the Ravens’ shakiest area with second-year kicker Tyler Loop missing an early 49-yard field goal and rookie punter Ryan Eckley shanking his first pro attempt for just 31 yards. Both bounced back later in the game, but their performance did little to quell questions about the team’s specialists. Minter also gave a “major shout-out” to undrafted rookie quarterback Joe Fagnano, who completed 22 of his 28 passes for 224 yards, one touchdown, and one interception. Minter even downplayed the turnover, saying that he “liked the throw that he made” and crediting Eagles cornerback Kelee Ringo for making a great play. Fagnano admitted in the locker room that he should not have attempted the aggressive cross-body pass on second down in the red zone. But that was the lone mistake from an otherwise impressive NFL debut by the former UConn starter who was thrust into Baltimore’s third-string quarterback role after Skylar Thompson suddenly landed on injured reserve this week. Backup quarterback Tyler Huntley, who got the start with Lamar Jackson resting, completed six of his seven passes. Five were caught by rookie pass-catchers, including a 29-yard wheel route from fourth-round tight end Matt Hibner that really got the offense going. Big play to @MatthewHibner to get things started!! Tune in on @wbaltv11 pic.twitter.com/Ci16UyZol2 — Baltimore Ravens (@Ravens) August 15, 2026 “I kind of blacked out after the catch,” Hibner said, adding that he may have celebrated too much with fellow rookie Ja’Kobi Lane. Lane, a third-round pick, took his turn in the spotlight, too. He has dazzled with near-daily highlights at training camp and added to his summer tally with an 18-yard grab from Huntley early on and capping his night with a 16-yard touchdown from Fagnano. Not to be outdone, Elijah Sarratt led the offense with six catches and 66 yards, though he did lose a fumble while trying to pick up extra yards after the catch. Sarratt said that his coaches and teammates – veterans and rookies alike – found him on the sidelines after the turnover and told him to keep his head up. After the game, Huntley said that the Ravens’ rookie pass-catchers “came ready to play and showed their talent today.” First-round guard Vega Ioane also impressed in his NFL debut, generally holding up in pass protection including this physical rep against Eagles edge rusher Arnold Ebeketie: CLEAROUT BLOCK BY @vegaioane17 . 😳 Tune in now on @wbaltv11 . pic.twitter.com/sZKpHVRXLW — Baltimore Ravens (@Ravens) August 15, 2026 Ioane played just two series, but that was all Ravens fans needed to see after the team’s guard woes over the last few years. They can rest easy knowing that Jackson will be well-protected this year, at least from the right guard spot. Center is a different story altogether. The Ravens have been searching for their new starter ever since Tyler Linderbaum left in free agency. They narrowly missed out on multiple coveted prospects during the draft and instead have turned to a hodgepodge of players to compete for the starting job. Former Colts backup Danny Pinter got the start vs. Philadelphia, followed by Jovaughn Gwyn, who came to Baltimore from Atlanta with offensive line coach Dwayne Ledford. Ex-Browns starter Ethan Pocic did not come into the game until the fourth quarter, though he is coming off a torn Achilles and has had significantly less time in the Ravens offense than his competition. Saturday night’s game did little to solidify any player’s grip on the starting center job. Minter and Doyle have both said they want to give Pocic a fair shot once he is back to 100% physically and fully up to speed in the offense. Taking the field tonight is a sign of progress on both fronts, so joint practices and the team’s second preseason game in Minnesota should offer some more answers.
author: Nikhil Mehta

title: Beatdown Roundtable: Reactions to the Ravens’ preseason win over the Eagles
summary: The Baltimore Ravens earned a 24-7 win in their 2026 preseason opener, securing a wire-to-wire victory in Jesse Minter’s head coaching debut. Here is the Baltimore Beatdown staff’s reaction to the win: A very encouraging start to Jesse Minter’s debut season. The offense looked smooth and got the young skill guys active early while the […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MD - AUGUST 15: Tyler Huntley #5 of the Baltimore Ravens attempts a pass against the Philadelphia Eagles during the first half of the preseason game at M&T Bank Stadium on August 15, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Scott Taetsch/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens earned a 24-7 win in their 2026 preseason opener, securing a wire-to-wire victory in Jesse Minter’s head coaching debut. Here is the Baltimore Beatdown staff’s reaction to the win: A very encouraging start to Jesse Minter’s debut season. The offense looked smooth and got the young skill guys active early while the defense completely shut down the Eagles offense. Ja’Kobi Lane, Elijah Sarratt, and Matthew Hibner showed flashes of their potential roles in Declan Doyle’s offense. A few UDFA’s made strong impressions, with Joe Fagnano being the standout. Looking forward to seeing more growth in the next two games. — Mark Myers While you can never glean much from any preseason game, there was a lot to like for the Ravens against the Eagles. Multiple young players impressed, including rookies Vega Ioane, Ja’Kobi Lane, Elijah Sarratt, Mathew Hibner, and Joe Fagnano. The defense was suffocating and nearly pitched a shutout, which makes me even more excited to see what the starting unit can do in Week 1 under Jesse Minter. The only real wart on the night for me was the missed field goal by Tyler Loop. Loop is under extreme pressure in his second season after a missed field goal ended Baltimore’s playoff hopes last season, and tonight’s blunder will only give more life to criticism. — Dustin Cox The Jesse Minter era got off to a great start as the Ravens secured a comfortable preseason victory, something the franchise has done plenty of times over the years. Tyler Huntley performed well in starting action at quarterback and the Ravens received promising showings from their rookie offensive class. Elijah Sarratt, Matthew Hibner and Jakobi Lane led the team in receiving, while Adam Randall rushed for 46 yards with a touchdown. On defense, cornerback Keyon Martin helped boost his stock further with a starring performance. The defense as a whole was dominant, not allowing a score until late in the fourth quarter with the game out of reach. Here’s hoping this sets the stage for more stalwart defensive outings for the 2026 season. — Frank Platko
author: Frank Platko

title: Ravens Stock Report: Rookie pass-catchers thrive, specialists struggle
summary: The Baltimore Ravens got their first action of the 2026 season on Saturday night with a preseason matchup against the Philadelphia Eagles. The result of the game – a 24-7 Ravens win – matters a lot less than the strides (and stumbles) by several players jockeying for a 53-man roster spot and regular-season playing time. […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MD - AUGUST 15: Ja'kobi Lane #6 of the Baltimore Ravens dives for a receiving touchdown against Michael Carter II #35 and Kelee Ringo #7 of the Philadelphia Eagles during the first half of the preseason game at M&T Bank Stadium on August 15, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Scott Taetsch/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens got their first action of the 2026 season on Saturday night with a preseason matchup against the Philadelphia Eagles. The result of the game – a 24-7 Ravens win – matters a lot less than the strides (and stumbles) by several players jockeying for a 53-man roster spot and regular-season playing time. Here’s the latest stock report out of M&T Bank Stadium from Baltimore Beatdown’s staff: Stock Up TE Matthew Hibner After much talk about the lackluster performance from the tight end room this training camp, Hibner eases concerns ever so slightly with a big catch down the field on the opening drive. The rookie continued with two nice catch-and-run plays on consecutive drives, showing a bit a burst in the process. – Dustin Cox OLB Adisa Isaac Because of his lengthy absences, Isaac needed to put something positive on film to make a case for the team to continue investing in him. The play didn’t count, but he showed good instincts and hustle snagging a ball for a would-be pick-six. – Kevin McNelis WRs Ja’Kobi Lane Lane’s stock was already about as high as it could be for a mid-round rookie after an excellent training camp, but he continued that into the first preseason game with a touchdown on his third catch of the game. Lane appears ready to play a sizeable role in the offense once the regular season arrives. – Dustin Cox CB Keyon Martin Martin has looked good tonight as well. He was all over the field from the first drive, drawing a holding penalty and flying across the formation to stop a WR run. He kept going in the second half with a TFL and a sack to snuff out a drive almost entirely on his own. – Nikhil Mehta QBs Tyler Huntley and Joe Fagnano Huntley was his usual self as one of the better backup quarterbacks in the league, but it was third-stringer Fagnano that impressed in the first preseason game. Outside of an interception in the endzone, the undrafted rookie was cool, calm, and collected, displaying control of the offense while getting the ball to his playmakers. After watching Devin Leary in recent preseasons, Fagnano has been a welcome surprise. – Dustin Cox Stock Down K Tyler Loop Following a missed field goal that cost the Ravens a trip to the postseason, Loop missing a 49-yard field goal to open the preseason should only magnify the pressure on the second-year kicker. He came back later to convert from 42 yards, but fans may start clamoring for some veteran competition. – Dustin Cox OL Emery Jones Jr. Jones was beat multiple times in pass protection early in the game, including once by Eagles DT Ty Robinson that resulted in a Huntley sack. He saw time at both guard spots, but not tackle, where the Ravens badly need some depth. – Nikhil Mehta Jesse Minter’s new defense While it’s just the preseason, you couldn’t hope for more in the debut of Minter’s (and Anthony Weaver’s) defense as the unit nearly pitched a shutout with Philly’s only points coming with 2:14 left in the game. The Raven were suffocating throughout the night, making every play difficult for the Eagles’ offense, which managed just 159 yards on 40 plays (4.0 yards per play). They converted just six first downs all night with a 0-9 mark on third down. Baltimore’s coverage in the secondary was extremely strong, allowing the front seven to do their jobs. This performance should only make fans more excited for Minter’s defense once the regular season arrives. – Dustin Cox Rollercoaster WR Elijah Sarratt Sarratt was excellent for much of the night, reeling in six of his seven targets for 66 yards. However, he left the football unprotected after one catch and lost a fumble while trying to pick up some extra yards. The fourth-round pick handled his return opportunities fine, but turnovers are one of the quickest ways for rookies to get stuck on the bench. – Nikhil Mehta P Ryan Eckley Eckley’s first punt was…not good. It flew just 27 yards and went out of bounds at the Eagles’ 31-yard line. But the rookie’s second attempt had plenty of hang time and forced a fair catch at the Eagles’ 10. Tyler Loop made four of his five kicks on the night, so Eckley took care of his holding duties, too. But Baltimore will want more consistency out of Jordan Stout’s successor. – Nikhil Mehta

Here’s what Baltimore Beatdown’s staff will be watching during the game: I predict that the Ja’Kobi Lane hype train will continue rolling tonight with a highlight contested catch that he has become known for throughout training camp. I also predict that rookie running back Adam Randall will have a strong showing as he should be set for a sizeable workload from the backfield. On defense, I think Zion Young and Chandler Rivers will boost their stock in their first NFL game action. I am excited to see how involved the pair of rookie tight ends will be in the passing attack tonight, as the position has become a concern following an uneventful training camp from veteran Mark Andrews. – Dustin Cox In the preseason opener, I’m most excited to see what impact the Ravens’ rookie offensive skill position players can have. Ja’Kobi Lane, Elijah Sarratt and both rookie tight ends should see plenty of targets in the passing game. Lane will draw the most eyes as the star of training camp thus far. However, I’m especially keen on whether Matthew Hibner or Josh Cuevas can flash as NFL-ready pass catchers at tight end. It will also be interesting to see how running back Adam Randall performs. Randall has the potential to climb the running back depth chart and usurp Rasheen Ali for the No. 3 role with a strong preseason. – Frank Platko As much as we all want Ja’Kobi Lane to ball out, I’m fully preparing myself to see him end the day with 2 catches for 17 yards and have all of NFL media rambling about how he was overhyped. He’ll get more play as the offseason progresses. I’d expect to see a lot of play from LaJohntay Wester and Tez Walker as the offensive staff tries to see where they can be best utilized in Declan Doyle’s scheme. Ditto for the rookie tight ends, who will bear close observation. So far, the offensive staff hasn’t tipped their hands about how these tight ends are going to be deployed, and I want to see what Cuevas and Hibner do tonight. The defense is going to be fun, even if it’s the blandest version of what Coach Minter wants to dial up. I’m excited to see what the DBs do, especially Bilhal Kone and Robert Longerbeam, who could provide some depth as the season progresses. The player I’d expect to see play a ton is Adisa Isaac. He’s been heavily involved in the rotations of the ones and twos at practice, and I think the coaches are still trying to see what they have in him. The most important element tonight is going to be what they’ve emphasized in practice: the basics. How is their timing and tempo? Are they communicating effectively? Are guys getting their assignments right? Can they be disciplined? – Kevin McNelis Im excited to see Ja’Kobi Lane in game action. I wasn’t low on Lane but I never saw him being much of an early contributer outside of an occasional deep shot and a red zone role. I don’t know if he’ll have a magical play tonight but I would bet on seeing some poor backup corner committing a DPI on Lane trying to figure out how to cover that 6’4 contested catch monster. Bilhal Kone is another guy I’m extremely excited to watch. He had an excellent camp last year and even made a play in his lone preseason action, breaking up a pass before landing bad and causing his injury. He’s going to have to fight to make this roster but he’s exactly the type of corner that fits in Minter’s system, long, athletically, and a nose for being around the ball. The OL rotation will be fun to see as well. The center battle is the biggest one in camp and I imagine we see everybody get some run. First-round rookie Vega Ioane will make his debut and should absolutely bully some dudes. I’m high on Carson Vinson’s ability to eventually take over for Ronnie Stanley as the franchise left tackle and can’t wait to see his year 1 to year 2 jump with Ledford coaching him up. – Zach Canter

title: 3 things to watch for in the Ravens’ 1st preseason game
summary: It’s the start of a new era of football in Baltimore. The Ravens have their first preseason game on deck with a new head coach, new coaching staff, new jerseys, new stadium upgrades and more. Are you really a football fan if you don’t overreact to how your team does in its first game action, […]
full_text: It’s the start of a new era of football in Baltimore. The Ravens have their first preseason game on deck with a new head coach, new coaching staff, new jerseys, new stadium upgrades and more. Are you really a football fan if you don’t overreact to how your team does in its first game action, even if it is preseason? That being said, try not to let it sway your opinion on this team too much just yet. Here’s what we are looking out for in today’s matchup against the Eagles. Ja’Kobi Lane The Ja’Kobi Lane Hype Train (trademark pending) left the station early in training camp and has blown past original expectations. It’s no surprise that Lane has become a fan favorite. His Day 2 draft status paired with his personality, social media presence, and college highlight tape is perfect fuel for early excitement. But he’s lived up to the hype with true on-field talent so far. There are limits to what offseason practices and training camp can prove, but Lane has done everything he can to dominate. He has made a highlight-reel play seemingly every single day of camp, sometimes with multiple spectacular catches. And it’s not just grabbing fans’ attention. Even his quarterback, his teammates, and his coaches are only pouring more gas on the fire, rare for a non-first-round rookie. Lane has earned his way to first-team reps in camps, sideline conversations with Lamar Jackson at a frequent rate, and seemingly a much larger role than most expected from the third-round rookie. While it’s only practice so far, Lane can’t do much more until now. The next step in keeping the hype train chugging down the track is for it to appear in game action. Be ready for the Ravens to force-feed targets to Lane early tomorrow as they try to check off another box before the start of the season. If the rookie is going to have a sizeable role, they want as many examples of him earning it as possible. Preseason game action is the final box before the regular season arrives. OMG @cantGuardJak1 😮‍💨😮‍💨😮‍💨 pic.twitter.com/X2nkgB7bxd — Baltimore Ravens (@Ravens) August 4, 2026 The Tight End Room There aren’t many weak points to pick at this offense. The wide receivers are showing out, Dwayne Ledford is a steady hand leading the offensive line, Derrick Henry is Derrick Henry, and Lamar Jackson is Lamar Jackson. That leaves the tight end room as the unit’s major potential hole. There’s plenty of concern after Isaiah Likely and Charlie Kolar left in free agency, but the team still has Mark Andrews and restocked with veteran Durham Smythe and rookies Matt Hibner and Josh Cuevas. But if Ja’Kobi Lane has been the highlight of the camp, the tight end room has been the lowlight. So far, we haven’t seen the typical Andrews dominance we’ve usually seen in camp since 2019. Smythe has looked solid as a blocker but offers little as a pass-catcher. Hibner and Cuevas, both Day 3 picks, are not focal points of a new offensive scheme that is more wide-receiver-heavy than previous systems. At this point, I think it’s fair to say we know what to expect from Andrews and Smythe. Smythe will mostly be a blocking specialist, and Andrews isn’t the same explosive, downfield YAC tight end he used to be. That can still work. In this new system, the wideouts will do most of the heavy lifting, so Andrews needs to do what he does best: find the soft spots in zone and use his connection with Lamar Jackson to be a quarterback-friendly target, especially in the red zone. Don’t expect either veteran to get much run time in early preseason action, but you should be on the lookout for either of these rookie tight ends to make an impact. With a massive shakeup in this room, there are absolutely targets and roles to be had. The question is, can either of these rookies earn those targets and start to separate themselves? The Ravens are likely going to need one of these rookie tight ends to become an explosive option if this offense is to reach its full potential. Tight Ends Coach Zack Grossi on rookie tight ends @JCuev_80 and @MatthewHibner pic.twitter.com/KBdkiId9MG — Baltimore Ravens (@Ravens) August 11, 2026 Cornerback Depth It will never not be an issue. As the great Ozzie Newsome said, “You can never have enough corners.” The depth has already been tested in camp, with both Nate Wiggins and Marlon Humphrey dealing with injuries. Luckily, it sounds like neither is serious and shouldn’t impact their Week 1 status. But it’s a suddenly sobering thought to realize that might be a possibility to happen midseason, especially given Chidobe Awuzie’s injury history. Third-year corner T.J. Tampa has had another fantastic camp so far, like last year, and firmly planted himself as the top backup behind the top three starters and might force Jesse Minter to use a four-cornerback rotation instead of three. Beyond that, there are questions. Fifth-round rookie Chandler Rivers is a roster lock. It’s also hard to envision this team not including Keyon Martin, who made it last year as a UDFA and has put together a strong camp. That’s six corners making the roster already; where do the Ravens go from there? If the Ravens do keep a seventh cornerback, there’s plenty of options. Bilhal Kone and Robert Longerbeam, 2025 late-round picks who missed the entire season due to torn ACLs, have impressed so far. Kone especially had a great camp last year before his preseason injury last year and is a prototype for Minter’s defense with his size and athleticism. There are other names such as Marquise Robinson, Lardarius Webb Jr., and veteran Amani Oruwariye. If the Ravens do keep an additional corner, one of those guys will have to force the issue on a crowded roster. Watch that rotation and play in the first preseason action and going forward. . @Tamp1A 😤 pic.twitter.com/mY9cfta6Xq — Baltimore Ravens (@Ravens) August 6, 2026

title: Josh Allen, Keon Coleman shine in Buffalo Bills 2026 preseason debut
summary: The Buffalo Bills opened their 2026 NFL preseason slate at home against the Carolina Panthers, and while the final score might not matter, there is plenty to be gleaned from individual player performances. Sometimes, the performance is even less important than the time of the game a player was on the field. In the early […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - AUGUST 15: Princely Umanmielen #3 of the Carolina Panthers looks to sack Josh Allen #17 of the Buffalo Bills during the first half at Highmark Stadium on August 15, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Timothy T Ludwig/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills opened their 2026 NFL preseason slate at home against the Carolina Panthers, and while the final score might not matter, there is plenty to be gleaned from individual player performances. Sometimes, the performance is even less important than the time of the game a player was on the field. In the early going, at least, the Bills looked good. Their first-team offense was humming, and their first-team defense stifled the Panthers. It wasn’t until both teams’ backups entered the fray that the Panthers began to mount some competitive drives. Evaluating a preseason output always comes with one very large grain of salt, but our stock report for Buffalo’s first preseason game has both highs and lows. Horns Up: Keon Coleman For the embattled former second-round pick, a pivotal third season awaits. No judgment can be had after just one preseason game, but it was a nice afternoon for No. 0. Coleman started the game, and he saw plenty of action in the early going. Coleman was targeted four times, tied with DJ Moore and Ray Davis for the most first-half targets of any Bills wideout. Coleman caught all four of those passes, and while they amounted to just 17 yards, he did catch the first touchdown at New Highmark Stadium. Coleman kept moving while Josh Allen did Josh Allen things on a first-and-goal from the nine. Coleman also displayed his ability as a blocker, sealing the edge on a nice reverse to Mecole Hardman Jr. Thanks in part to his efforts, Hardman gained 27 yards on the play. Overall, it was a positive afternoon for Coleman. Horns Down: OTs not named Dion Dawkins On Buffalo’s first drive, it was right tackle Spencer Brown whiffing on Jaelan Phillips, resulting in a pressure on Josh Allen that forced a field goal attempt. On Buffalo’s second drive, Brown was shoved into Allen’s lap on a pass that was ultimately completed; however, it would have been nice to have kept QB1 on his feet on the play. Later, it was Chase Lundt and Jude Bowry allowing a defensive meeting in the Buffalo backfield, as both players whiffed on blocks that caused a major pressure on Kyle Allen. Later in the first half, Bowry was burned off the edge again, leading to a hit on Kyle Allen. He also committed a hold on Buffalo’s first drive of the third quarter, negating a long Frank Gore Jr. run. I don’t think it’s cause for major concern, but neither Lundt nor Bowry looked capable of stepping in against backups, let alone starters, in the event of an injury to either Brown or Dawkins. Horns Up: Quarterbacks with the surname Allen Both Josh Allen and Kyle Allen looked excellent all afternoon. Josh started the game, and he completed 6-of-8 passes for 111 yards and a score over his two drives. Three of those passes went to his newest target, DJ Moore, for 61 yards. The play-action pass, in particular, looked fantastic, as Allen hit Moore for one long gain and Khalil Shakir for two long gains off of hard play-fakes. Most importantly is that No. 17 exited the game with zero injuries. Kyle Allen took over on Buffalo’s third drive, and he was very efficient with the reserve group. He completed 14-of-16 passes for 108 yards during his work in the first half. Sure, there were plenty of check-downs to players like Ray Davis, but he threw a few nice passes to Trent Sherfield Sr., as well, who caught both of his first-half targets for 12 yards. Stephen Gosnell caught a pair of 18-yard strikes from No. 11, as well. It was a positive outing for the veteran backup. Horns Down: Geno Stone It was not a great first half for the veteran safety, as he allowed a passing touchdown late in the first half on the same drive where he committed a facemask penalty to extend it. Stone grabbed quarterback Kenny Pickett’s facemask on a third down near Carolina’s 20-yard line when the Buffalo stop unit had him dead to rights. That likely would have led to a punt. Instead, the Panthers had a first down on their own 37, and after a long pass interference penalty on Toriano Pride Jr., they had marched down the field and scored. Horns Up: Lloyd Cushenberry Sometimes, it’s when a guy doesn’t play that tells us more about a player than when or how he does play. Cushenberry started the game, but he came out when Josh Allen exited the game. Conversely, Sedrick Van Pran-Granger played deep into the second half. That tells me that Cushenberry is likely ahead of the third-year man in the race to back up Connor McGovern. Given that McGovern is currently nursing a hamstring injury, if he’s unable to go on September 13 when the Bills face the Houston Texans, I’d bet that it will be Cushenberry starting that game in his place. Horns Down: Discipline There were far too many sloppy penalties. Yes, it’s the first preseason game. Yes, many of those penalties were on young players. However, there was at least one penalty on a starter, as well, with Dion Dawkins jumping early for a false start. That’s been a major problem for him over the last few seasons. Maybe I’m just a crabby coach, but there were too many plays where a penalty ruined what otherwise looked like a solid rep. Horns Up: Dorian Williams See my earlier note regarding Lloyd Cushenberry. Dorian Williams started the game and made three first-half tackles. However, he was nowhere near the field in the second half, as rookie Kaleb Elarms-Orr and third-year man Joe Andreessen were playing late in the game. While that might have been a good sign for the rookie, it was a little interesting to see Andreessen on the field late in the third quarter and early in the fourth quarter. However, it looked like Dorian Williams is the clubhouse leader to start inside at linebacker next to Terrel Bernard. Horns Up: Jordan Hancock The second-year man was out there with the second-team defense, but he was all over the place when he was on the field. Hancock made four tackles, including two tackles for loss, and he looked good both in coverage and as a blitzer attacking the line of scrimmage. Steve Tasker noted on the broadcast that a change in defensive philosophy could be the best thing to happen to someone like Hancock, and while it’s only one afternoon, the early returns seem to support that point. Horns Questionable: T.J. Sanders and Mike Danna On the one hand, Danna had two sacks and essentially ended a fourth-quarter Carolina drive by himself. However, as a six-year veteran who played a key role on the Kansas City Chiefs’ defense over the last few seasons, it is definitely noteworthy that Danna was playing in the fourth quarter. Could this performance catapult him to a different role next week? Time will tell, but Danna definitely acquitted himself well in the role he was asked to play. As for Sanders, the team’s unofficial preseason depth chart listed him as a starter on the defensive line; however, he was also playing well into the fourth quarter. There are only so many bodies, but after an up-and-down rookie season that was arguably more down than up, it’s not a great sign that he was playing in the fourth quarter without accruing much of anything in the way of attention-grabbing plays. Horns Up: Ian Wheeler With all due respect for Frank Gore Jr., who turned in a characteristically solid performance today, Wheeler came in against essentially the same competition and offered a completely different gear than the third-year man. Whereas Gore Jr. is patient but lacking in burst, Wheeler showed great vision, solid contact balance. Most importantly, he showed a second gear that Gore Jr. just doesn’t have. If Ty Johnson takes longer than anticipated to heal from his hamstring injury, Wheeler could start to position himself as a possible third running back with more outings like this. I’ll be…

(Photo by Timothy T Ludwig/Getty Images) | Getty Images Buffalo Bills football is back, Rumblers! Well, okay, it’s just preseason football and only the first game of the exhibition period. But still, football is finally back in its evaluative form. Bills Mafia is understandably excited to see what’s in store during the 2026 NFL season. For the first time in just shy of a decade, the team has a new, and first-time, head coach in Joe Brady. He previously served as the team’s offensive coordinator before being named head coach this past offseason. The defense will also look vastly different than it has in ages thanks to new, first-time NFL defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard. A grain of preseason salt is always required in these moments. Everything is going to look vanilla at best, simply because teams are unwilling to put out film on their intentions before necessary. Coaches also use these scrimmages as a deeper evaluation period as it relates to roster management. Don’t expect a lot of gamesmanship. Of course among the biggest items of news is the team’s brand-new Highmark Stadium, which opened last weekend to fans during the “Return of the Blue & Red” practice. Today is different, though, and it’s the first chance for folks around the country to see the new stadium on the big screen. With that, it’s once again time to pass the football your way with this open thread. Join in the conversation this afternoon as the Bills take on the Carolina Panthers! This season, we’re going to keep game-day threads to one post to keep everyone engaged in the same place. As always, be kind to one another — and in all things… Go Bills!

summary: Last week, the Buffalo Bills hosted their first public event at Highmark Stadium with the annual Return of the Blue & Red practice. full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - OCTOBER 26: Greg Rousseau #50 of the Buffalo Bills sacks Andy Dalton #14 of the Carolina Panthers during the NFL 2025 game between the Buffalo Bills and the Carolina Panthers at Bank of America Stadium on October 26, 2025 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Kara Durrette/Getty Images) | Getty Images Last week, the Buffalo Bills hosted their first public event at Highmark Stadium with the annual Return of the Blue & Red practice. Later this afternoon, the Bills will play their first football game in their new stadium when Buffalo welcomes the Carolina Panthers to Western New York for a 1 p.m. kickoff in Week 1 of the preseason. We know that Josh Allen “would love to play” in Buffalo’s preseason opener, and that new defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard expects his starters to “let it rip” against Carolina. But what else can Bills fans expect in the preseason opener for both teams? Today’s edition of Buffalo Rumblinks leads off by previewing the key players to watch when Buffalo and Carolina square off this afternoon. Check out the assessments and then be sure to let us know in the comments section what you will be watching for when the Bills play their preseason opener. What can Bills fans expect in Week 1 of preseason? One of the biggest issues a team has to handle in the preseason is how much to play their starters, especially in the preseason opener. If Josh Allen gets his wish, he will start in Week 1 with the rest of Buffalo’s first-stringers in the first game action with Joe Brady as head coach. “I would love to play,” Allen said after practice on Thursday. “I couldn’t tell you how long or how many drives or what’s the case there, but to get out there and get a good feeling and a good sense of the game and a good sense of the guys around me, I feel like that’s important to do.” Brady echoed those sentiments, telling reporters before Thursday’s practice that he plans on playing all of his healthy starters for at least a little bit vs. the Panthers. “Everybody that’s healthy is going to be playing out there on Saturday,” Brady said Thursday. “I want to see guys get hit, I want to see guys tackle, I want to see the finishing of the play and all of this. There’s so many variables with it. We obviously have a new everything, right, so it’s our first opportunity for us to come together and show an example of what the Buffalo Bills are about, too, so I think that’s important.” We run through some of the positional battles and key players to watch in Week 1 of the preseason; see how the preseason will determine who claims the backup QB job between Kyle Allen and Shane Buechele; learn how defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard expects his starters to “let it rip” in the preseason opener; share how Bills fans can watch the game from home; and more! title: Thurman Thomas & 34 Group, Inc. key to Bills’ new Highmark Stadium construction
summary: Thurman Thomas is a legend and an icon whose tenacity and grit coupled with truly awe-inspiring traits as a shifty dual-threat running back paved the way for an NFL Hall of Fame career that lasted 12 seasons with the Buffalo Bills. The franchise’s Super Bowl teams were perhaps as much defined by Thomas’ work as […]
full_text: Thurman Thomas is a legend and an icon whose tenacity and grit coupled with truly awe-inspiring traits as a shifty dual-threat running back paved the way for an NFL Hall of Fame career that lasted 12 seasons with the Buffalo Bills. The franchise’s Super Bowl teams were perhaps as much defined by Thomas’ work as anyone else on the roster. Teams simply weren’t ever quite sure when or where Thomas was going to make them pay, what his next move was from play to play. Keeping up with Thurman Thomas proved far more difficult than anyone had predicted. That proved even more remarkable when years after his retirement Thomas revealed that he played his entire NFL career with a partially torn ACL in his left knee. That’s sheer grit and determination, like few others then or now. At a position with so much franchise star power through various generations, Thomas continues to rise above the rest. He was the complete package on the field then, and he remains so decades after having taken his last handoff in a Bills uniform. For a man who’s now spent half his life in Western New York, it might be easy to look back and say he’s done it all. Yet, if you ask Thomas, he’d likely tell you he’s just getting started. In a recent conversation with Thurman that set out intent on covering as much ground as was true of his tremendous career, we were drawn to the here and now. For at this moment, something special is unfolding for the whole of Bills Mafia. In case you haven’t read the headlines or opened social media in some weeks, One Bills Drive has cut the ribbon on their new home, a completely new, from the ground up, version of Highmark Stadium. In fact, the franchise just held its first public event for season ticket holders and other lucky fans of the team. In holding its annual “Return of the Blue & Red” practice, the Bills showed more than 50,000 die-hard supporters what all the fuss was about in that giant structure taking shape the last three years across Abbott Road. Interestingly enough, that’s where Thomas’ connection here takes shape. While his jersey and number have been retired and adorn the inside of the new Highmark Stadium, that’s not his only place of prominence within its walls. Truth be told, Thomas has his name displayed and honored in three separate places inside the new stadium, plus as part of the ring of honor outside the stadium’s confines in what’s known as the Family Circle. Yet, the why and where of Thomas’ name being included so many places isn’t immediately obvious outside of his football career. In speaking with him, the story of a poignant full-circle moment unfolds that finds Thomas continually give back to the community that lifted him on its shoulders. 34 Group, Inc. helping build better for Buffalo, and the Bills Thurman and his wife Patti Thomas established 34 Group, Inc. in Buffalo, NY in 2016. Construction has been a massive part of Patti’s family for decades, with her father Robert Mariacher establishing a construction company in the 1950s that played an instrumental role in helping to develop the greater Buffalo, NY area in the coming decades. As a small business and commercial construction company, 34 Group is a “ New York State Certified Minority Business Enterprise (MBE) providing design, construction management and self-performed construction services. ” Coincidentally, 34 Group was also one of the companies chosen to help with construction of the Bills’ new stadium. Thomas understands the challenges facing any startup, noting the necessary hill climb, and “to be an up-and-coming new group in the Buffalo area, it was a struggle at first.” The company wasn’t focused on the large prize at first, with Thomas saying “we were confident that we were going to be just a small company — just helping out, really. I mean, because, to have something like a stadium built, we couldn’t handle that on our own. And that was Turner and Gilbane [joint venture construction management team Gilbane Building Company and Turner Construction Company] who led the charge for getting everybody set.” Even after this project, Thomas maintains that “we were just the little guys, you know, but we put in all 60 thousand of the seats in the new Highmark Stadium, courtesy of Irwin [ Irwin Seating Company ]. And they’ve done an outstanding job with us,” while adding that 34 Group also “did some stuff for the grass field.” Focusing exclusively on commercial projects has allowed the Thomases and 34 Group to build a deeper connection with people in Buffalo. Thomas welcomes that bond, saying that it’s been really helpful and “gotten me back into the community.” With that community comes projects of all sizes for 34 Group. “Yeah, sure, this was a $2.2 billion job for this stadium, but for our company — we take the $50,000 dollar jobs, we take the $100,000 dollar jobs. Thomas constantly strives to capture something beneficial in any endeavor, stating of a any potential project that ”it’s that relationship that I always tell my employees that we’re not going to win every single job, but make sure you have a relationship, a communication person you can always talk to, because something’s always going to pop up.” It’s clear Thomas is happy diving into his work with 34 Group, saying that “it’s been great, man. I love doing the work around here in the Buffalo area. Thomas maintains that 34 Group is about so much more than the next project. “I mean it’s opened so many doors to where — not that we get work — but it’s opened so many doors for other things, and I think that’s the most important thing, besides our company, is the relationship that we have with the folks in the Buffalo area.” For Thomas, it’s perhaps a passion project like no other yet, and one that fate helped connect to his prior career. In asking Thomas about the experience of working alongside other construction outfits and contractors, he said “it’s been a really good experience for a lot of the companies in the Buffalo area because I think everybody got a piece of [the action] to do something. I think that was kind of the thing that when we [began building] this stadium — we wanted everybody to get a piece of it. Right? And I think everybody did.” Thomas humbly defers to the expertise and work of the tradespeople within 34 Group. Again, it’s a team that undertook the installation of each and every seat — all 60,129 of those red and blue seats — in the new Highmark Stadium. It’s an accomplishment he wears proudly upon his sleeve, and something that continues to fuel each and every return trip. “I’ve been over there probably five or six times in the last couple of weeks and they’re still tweaking some things or whatever,” Thomas said. A clear sign that despite the already finished look there is still much to do before the regular season is ushered in. What stands out to him in speaking with folks around town is the sheer magnitude of the project. “From what I’m hearing, a lot of the positives are that people are saying: ‘Is this really in Buffalo? Is this type of stadium really in Buffalo?,’” Thomas quipped. “To me, I think it’s night and day when you talk about the old Highmark and you talk about the new Highmark. This one here, it’s spectacular, there’s a lot to see in there and there’s a lot of room — a lot of space for the fans to walk around,” he added. Then in a nod to fans’ obvious passion for new place, Thomas with a smile on his face said that it was evident during the Blue & Red practice that “everybody wanted to walk around the stadium, right, to see everything — instead of being in their seats.” Honestly, who can blame them? Still, it’s noteworthy when quarterback Josh Allen is upstaged in any stadium. A positive attitude amid Highmark seating concerns With any public project, critiques are bound to catch fire as soon as folks find something to latch onto, either first-hand or from afar. Thomas understands where some fans are coming from in terms of slight-line concerns, but he’d prefer to let…

title: Panthers 14 Bills 29: An ugly day for the Panthers starting offense
summary: We finally got to see the Panthers trot out their first team offense and defense this week. It was not an easy watch but I will let you read along if you didn’t catch the game yourself! First Quarter Josh Allen and the starting offense marched down the field with a 21 yard pass to […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - AUGUST 15: Kenny Pickett #12 of the Carolina Panthers runs the ball during the second quarter a preseason game against the Buffalo Bills at Highmark Stadium on August 15, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images We finally got to see the Panthers trot out their first team offense and defense this week. It was not an easy watch but I will let you read along if you didn’t catch the game yourself! First Quarter Josh Allen and the starting offense marched down the field with a 21 yard pass to Khalil Shakir and a 32 yard catch and run by DJ Moore, before their offense was stopped by a Jaelan Phillips sack. The Bills kicked a field goal to start the game 3-0. The Bills mostly smothered the Panthers starting offense with a 3 and out as Bryce Young threw the ball to avoid a sack on 3rd down. The Bills drove the ball down the field with their 1’s as the Panthers started to shift out their first team defense. The Panthers almost had another 3rd down sack but Trevis Gipson was called for a face mask on the play, the Bills followed it up with a Josh Allen touchdown pass to Keon Coleman. The Panthers second drive with the first team didn’t go much better, as they went 3 and out once again after a batted Bryce Young pass on 3rd down. The Panthers old friend Kyle Allen took over for the Bills. Mecole Hardeman took a rush for 27 yards, but a Cam Gill sack and a containment of Kyle Allen ended the first quarter with a 4th and 3 decision. Second Quarter The Bills converted said 4th down rather easily to open the quarter. Trevin Wallace made the tackle short of the sticks on the next set of downs, setting up a Tyler Bass field goal attempt, which he missed. 10-0 Bills. The Panthers opened their second quarter on offense with the starters still in. They appeared to get a first down but were called for a penalty. What it was, I am not sure because I had to watch the Bills stream via the NFL app and the broadcast spent the entire drive talking about the Bills’ newest amenities (I hate the preseason). Another 3 and out. The Bills took the ball and once again drove into scoring range, but a tackle for a loss on 2nd and a gang sack on 3rd down forced another field goal attempt. Bass made this one, 13-0 Bills. Kenny Two Gloves Pickett took over for the ensuing drive. A facemask penalty granted the Panthers the first conversion of downs of the game. A nice completion to Jimmy Horn Jr and a Ja’Seem Reed drawn defensive pass interference play later and the Panthers were in scoring range. Scramble by Kenny Pickett brought the team to first and goal. Kenny hit Ja’Seem Reed for a touchdown to make it 13-7 Bills! The Bills offense didn’t get much of a chance as the half closed out, the Panthers pass rush got after Kyle Allen to not give him much time to throw. Third Quarter The Panthers offense kicked things off and they were moving with two straight first downs. They got to a 4th down following a Kenny Pickett sack, but they kept the offense out and converted on a pass to James Mitchell. The next few plays were disastrous, but the Panthers were bailed out on 3rd and very long by another DPI penalty. Unfortunately, they got to 4th and 2, went for it again, and the Bills batted Pickett’s pass. Turnover on downs. The Bills took it back with Shane Buechele at the helm, and a big DPI penalty on Corey Thornton but the Bills into scoring range. They were stalled, so another Bass field goal got the score to 16-7 Bills. Kenny Pickett remained in the game and capped the quarter off with a 20 catch and run by AJ Dillon. Fourth Quarter Two sacks including one on 4th down swiftly ended the Panthers drive. The Bills drove it down the field with mostly running plays, capped off by a Ian Wheeler rushing touchdown on goal to go, as the announcers on the Bills broadcast were talking about sandwiches and chicken wings the whole drive. The Bills went for it on the 2 point conversion after a penalty and missed out. 22-7 Bills. Kyle Trask took over for Carolina. Kyle threw a pick after a holding penalty, a screen pass that the Bills defense jumped. Frank Gore Jr ran it in for the Bills to continue piling on the scoreboard, Bills 29-7. Kyle Trask led a nice touchdown drive to wind down the game, with a pass to John Metchie. Bills up 29-14 Final Thoughts This game was a hard watch following the Hall of Fame Game. The Panthers starting offense went 3 and out on every drive they had, Jonathon Brooks was swallowed up on 2 of his 3 rushing attempts, and the offensive line as a whole didn’t look great at times. But, this is the preseason, so this is the time to work those kinks out. I was impressed with Trevis Gipson and Thomas Incoom as pass rushers during the day. Kenny Pickett did fine as a backup QB playing with the 2nd/3rd team offense. Share your thoughts down below on the preseason game!

title: Brian Answers: Haynes King rules all
summary: Hello CSR! Welcome to Brian Answers, part two of your weekly Panthers fan mailbag for everyone! It has been a heck of a week following the GREATEST HALL OF FAME GAME EVER, and we’re onto the Buffalo Bills, where we’ll get to see some Panthers starters for a change. I despise the preseason, but so […]
full_text: CANTON, OHIO - AUGUST 06: Haynes King #16 of the Carolina Panthers scores a five-yard touchdown to defeat the Arizona Cardinals 33-30 in the 2026 Pro Football Hall of Fame Game at Tom Benson Hall Of Fame Stadium on August 06, 2026 in Canton, Ohio. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Diamond Images via Getty Images) | Diamond Images/Getty Images Hello CSR! Welcome to Brian Answers, part two of your weekly Panthers fan mailbag for everyone! It has been a heck of a week following the GREATEST HALL OF FAME GAME EVER, and we’re onto the Buffalo Bills, where we’ll get to see some Panthers starters for a change. I despise the preseason, but so far this particular year has been quite fun. Let’s dive into your questions! @WTMealey: Two answers please to the same question because person asking is different How do you feel about the Panthers upcoming season? Answer 1-friend/aquiantance who know you are a Panthers fan, but is at best a casual fan of football in general and probably doesn’t know any players outside of Bryce maybe Tmac Answer 2-friend who is a hard core fan of both the NFL in general but also a hard core fan of another team-your choice who the other team is I feel pretty good about this season, but in the sense that the Panthers will be a team discussed more seriously by the national media than they have since possibly 2019. They may only win one more game than last year, but its nice to see non-Panthers fans taking notice for a change. Draft Jalen Coker in fantasy, bruh-ther! And Jonathon Brooks! Bruce Guild: Your thoughts on chances (in %) of King making the 53 before the HoF game and after? Do you think if King continues to show composure and ability demonstrated in the HoF game does it change Morgan’s, Tillis and Eager’s approach and mindset on any possible 2nd contract? Does it reduce pressure to sign at a premium knowing you may have a QB on the roster that can be developed with possible high upside? I went into the offseasons thinking Haynes King was a lock to make the practice squad after final roster cuts. And as you know, I am notoriously right about the training camp and preseason feel good stories who end up being cut. However, that performance did change my view, I do think Haynes King actually finds himself on the 53 man roster. He definitely adds a talent that the Panthers can use, both as a QB and as a gadget/package specific player. Now, in regards to Bryce Young, I don’t think Haynes King making the roster changes anything. King should not factor into the decision to give him an extension, its going to be 100% on Bryce. That decision is going to be figured out based on his performance this season. King doesn’t have anything to do with that. Might impact Kenny Pickett more than anything if I’m being honest. Revshawn: So now that a few days have passed after the epic performance of Haynes King and his heroic comeback on Thursday, what is the current opinion of Brian Beversluis’s on the matter as well as his future in Carolina? Do we got something cooking here? How is it possible for so many draft analysts to be so blind to the glory and the magnificence that is Haynes King? First of his name. King of the Queen City. Lord Command of the South. Guardian over the Mason Dixon line. I was very pleased with Haynes King. I felt he would need a lot more work to be able to throw consistently at the NFL level but he clearly put the work in, or the talent was already there. Sure, he’s not exactly young at 25 years old for a rookie, but its not like the Panthers burned a first round pick on him or anything like that. It seems that most analysts had questions for him as a passer, so that will continue to be my thing I want to see more of. But he certainly surprised me with his throws and poise in the pocket right away. For once, the CSR hype may have been warranted. JakeNCVA: What position/position group — if any — do you think the answer is not currently on the roster and that will be filled with other teams’ roster cuts or even a trade before the season starts? Its always funny with these mailbags, often the team does something in between that basically answers my question. I probably would have said tight end as one of the options, and the team went and agreed to terms on a one year deal* with TE Darren Waller out of the blue earlier in the week. That likely means they don’t believe in Ja’Tavion Sanders as the pass catching tight end of their multi-faceted group right now. I also believe they may bring in a linebacker on the inside during cuts. They are also known to grab interior offensive and defensive linemen for depth during the final roster cutdowns. Possibly a player in the secondary but so far I’ve been pretty impressed with most of the guys projected to make the roster. Mozzie11: On the taskbar of my computer on the left is the weather or a news blurb. When you hover over it a news aggregate feed pops up with news articles covering a wide range of topics. And right there in the feed this morning was ‘Ask Brian: The Panthers won a preseason game!’ Brian going big time. Congratulations to all posters who helped make this happen. I am sure checks will be mailed out soon. In a sideline reporter voice: So Brian how does this success make you feel? I words very good. But seriously, you all interacting and having discussions often helps these kinds of things. So that’s more of a testament to the community than anything! So comment down below with how the success makes YOU feel! Dcangio09: Well there it is Not a question, but a proper send off for this fan mailbag! Jalen Coker is the only WR drafted since 2020 who has 125+ yards and 1+ TDs in a playoff game, and he did it in his first one. CSR has gotten very good at recognizing UDFA talent before the rest of the world has caught on. Celebrate yourselves. ENJOY THE GAME TODAY AND KEEP POUNDING!

full_text: ATLANTA, GA JANUARY 05: Carolina offensive coordinator Brad Idzik embraces quarterback Bryce Young (9) during the NFL game between the Carolina Panthers and the Atlanta Falcons on January 5th, 2025 at Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta, GA. full_text: CHARLOTTE, NC - OCTOBER 25: Kawann Short #99 of the Carolina Panthers celebrates a sack against the Philadelphia Eagles in the 1st half during their game at Bank of America Stadium on October 25, 2015 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Streeter Lecka/Getty Images) | Getty Images Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #29. Kawann Short Kawann Short was part of an unorthodox draft class for the Carolina Panthers in 2013. After a standout career at Purdue, the Panthers picked him in the second round with the 44th overall pick. While there’s no problem picking up a quality defensive tackle in the second round, it came after the Panthers picked defensive Star Lotulelei in the first round. While the two played different roles and techniques, it was still somewhat unusual to see a team pick two players that nominally played the same position with each of their first two picks. It paid off though. For his part, Short was one of the most efficient pass rushers from the middle of the line across the entire NFL, and he helped contribute to a powerful front line that anchored one of the better defenses in the league. As time went on, Short got better at translating his disruptiveness into production. In his third season, he compiled 11 sacks, which led the team and earned him All Pro honors. That would prove to be his peak. He would compile 16.5 sacks over the next three seasons, though he would land a second Pro Bowl nomination in the third one. That would be his final healthy season. He played just two games in 2019 before a shoulder injury ended his season. His 2020 season would meet the same fate after three games. The Panthers released him at the end of the 2020 season, and that was the end of his NFL career. Prior to the recurring shoulder injuries that ultimately ended Short’s career, he was a true ironman that was a fixture on the Panthers front four. He was constantly disruptive in both phases of the game and was a perfect complement as a disruptor next to Lotulelei’s space eating style. The Panthers almost always had a good defense when Short was on the field, and that wasn’t a coincidence. And it’s not a coincidence that good defenses have been harder to find in Carolina since Short left. While he alone didn’t make the good defenses, he played a big part in them. For that, he lands at number 29 on the list of top 100 Panthers of all time.
