title: How concerned are Detroit Lions fans about the offensive line?
summary: Earlier this week, we published our latest SB Nation Reacts survey, sponsored by the folks at FanDuel Sportsbook, and asked Detroit Lions fans: What’s your concern level for the Lions’ offensive line after Cade Mays’ injury? Last week, Mays reportedly broke a small bone in his wrist and is expected to miss 8-10 weeks, meaning he […]
full_text: Detroit Lions offensive line coach Hank Fraley, center, talks to players at practice during training camp at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Monday, August 3, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co Earlier this week, we published our latest SB Nation Reacts survey, sponsored by the folks at FanDuel Sportsbook , and asked Detroit Lions fans: What’s your concern level for the Lions’ offensive line after Cade Mays’ injury? Last week, Mays reportedly broke a small bone in his wrist and is expected to miss 8-10 weeks, meaning he could return after the Lions’ Week 5 bye. The Lions have elected to explore their in-house replacement options and have leaned on Seth McLaughlin and Michael Niese as their next-up center options, while Juice Scruggs recovers from a soft tissue injury. With the future—at least the next two months—of the Lions center position up in the air, the concern level of the fan base was mixed: The poll ended with a slight lean toward optimism, and based on the comment section, it seems to be rooted in trust in the coaching staff to find the right replacement, while also having enough time to get them ready for the regular season. Let’s take a look a bit further into the comment section of our original article and The Feed post to see fans’ explanations for their selections (lightly edited for clarity). Waitingsince57 : “Moderate, and here’s why: 1) Holmes fortified the OL this offseason 2) The trade for Juice was certainly part of the plan for better interior depth, including Center 3) Seth is a formidable, award-winning Center from OSU just 2 years ago. He knows how to play the position. 4) Petzing and Hank will figure it out!” Enor : “It all starts with the middle of the line. I’m very concerned.” 12Jamie : “Concern level is pretty low. A team is very unlucky to get lots of injuries; a team is very lucky to get only a few. Most teams have a fair share. And the season is long. If the Lions are serious about being contenders, it’s how healthy they are in January that matters.” Hungry Lion : “Moderately High. I’m glad the Lions have Juice Scruggs, but it’s not the same level of play.” ULTIMATEpunisher007 : “I’m not as worried as I thought I would be. Juice should be able to hold it down the first quarter of the season. This isn’t nearly as bad as losing Frank.” PrideLander : “My level of concern is moderate, due primarily to the present uncertainty around the position. Fortunately, it is still early enough in the preseason to sort out a viable solution with Juice, Tate, or McLaughlin.” As a reminder, this survey was sponsored by the folks over at FanDuel Sportsbook , who currently have the Lions listed as +1900 to win this year’s Super Bowl, +900 to win the NFC Championship, and +150 to win the NFC North as the current favorites. Throughout the year, we ask questions of the most plugged-in Detroit Lions fans and fans across the country. If you want to receive these surveys by email weekly, you can sign up here .

title: Detroit Lions signing veteran running back amidst injuries
summary: Late Friday night, news broke that the Detroit Lions are signing veteran running back Trayveon Williams, according to Aaron Wilson. Williams was a sixth-round pick in 2019 for the Cincinnati Bengals. He stayed with the Bengals for six seasons, appearing in 68 games over that span, mostly serving on special teams, logging 873 snaps in […]
full_text: Cincinnati Bengals running back Trayveon Williams (32) runs during Bengals training camp on Aug. 6, 2019, in Cincinnati. Bengals Camp 42 | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co Late Friday night, news broke that the Detroit Lions are signing veteran running back Trayveon Williams, according to Aaron Wilson. Williams was a sixth-round pick in 2019 for the Cincinnati Bengals. He stayed with the Bengals for six seasons, appearing in 68 games over that span, mostly serving on special teams, logging 873 snaps in that phase. Some of those snaps were on kick returns, as he has a career total of 42 kick returns for 995 yards (an average of 22.7). That said, he only has 72 rushes and 343 rushing yards in his NFL career. As a running back, Williams is short (5-foot-8) but stocky (206 pounds). He gained a strong reputation in college for his tenacious attitude as a blocker, and a few very productive seasons at Texas A&M. In his junior and final year with the Aggies, he led the SEC with 1,760 rushing yards and 18 rushing touchdowns. The Lions could use a little depth at running back right now, as the position is currently filled with injuries. Detroit only had three running backs suited up on Thursday, with Isiah Pacheco, Sione Vaki, and Jabari Small sidelined with injuries and Jahmyr Gibbs resting. As of right now, the signing of Williams is not official, and no corresponding move has been announced by the team.
author: Jeremy Reisman

title: 5 Detroit Lions who hurt their roster chances in preseason opener
summary: NFL preseason is always a mixed bag, as teams dive into their depth chart to see which players will step up in the spotlight. Against the Cincinnati Bengals, the Detroit Lions had a fair number of good showings, but there are two sides to every coin and many players saw their roster chances take a […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OHIO - AUGUST 13: Luke Altmyer #2 of the Detroit Lions passes the ball during the first quarter of the preseason game against the Cincinnati Bengals at Paycor Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Cincinnati, Ohio. (Photo by Justin Casterline/Getty Images) | Getty Images NFL preseason is always a mixed bag, as teams dive into their depth chart to see which players will step up in the spotlight. Against the Cincinnati Bengals, the Detroit Lions had a fair number of good showings, but there are two sides to every coin and many players saw their roster chances take a hit. Whether due to a bad performance themselves or a good performance from their peers, there are some players on this Lions roster that walked away from Thursday night with more questions than answers. Will they be able to fight for a roster spot in the coming weeks? Previously: 5 Lions who helped their roster chances vs. Bengals Michael Niese, C While I was not overly impressed with Seth McLaughlin (who had partial responsibility for a sack allowed), it was unfortunately Niese that caught my attention for the wrong reason. Though he had a good block to spring Raheem Blackshear on a 24-yard run, I am concerned about him at center. He skipped a snap off the turf, resulting in a 5-yard loss, while another poor snap was salvaged by Luke Altmyer. The game-day conditions were wet, but a center needs to corral the football better. Am I picking on a player for two bad snaps? Perhaps, but as a center, that’s your primary responsibility. Last season, Niese stepped in mid-game at center, then promptly delivered a poor snap that ended up as a safety—that would end up being his last offensive snap of 2025. If Niese wants to make the roster (a realistic goal given the injuries to Cade Mays and Juice Scruggs), he needs to clean up all aspects of being a center. Dominic Lovett, WR Lovett tied for the team lead in receiving with three catches for 28 yards, but he left a lot to be desired. His three receptions came on a team-high eight targets, but the second-year receiver failed to haul in more than half of them, two of which were dropped. He was largely unimpactful on special teams as well, bobbling one of his two punt returns. Lovett is competing for both a wide receiver role and a special teams role, and given the competition at both, he needs to separate himself from the pack to justify a roster spot. To Lovett’s benefit, however, none of the other receivers stood out on Thursday either. Luke Altmyer, QB This is a complicated tape to judge because, in general, I was actually encouraged by Altmyer’s performance. I think he moved the ball downfield with some authority and had a fair number of excellent passes—his best came on a 23-yard dart to Cedrick Wilson. He had some poise in the pocket, and of his two interceptions, one was a drop by Isaac TeSlaa and the other was a hero ball in the dying seconds of the game (although still an off-target throw). However, this was perhaps Altmyer’s best opportunity to stake his claim ahead of Joshua Dobbs on the depth chart, and that did not happen. Neither quarterback dominated (Altmyer finished 13-of-22 with 130 yards, a touchdown, and the two picks, while Dobbs went 4-for-8 for 32 yards), but because Dobbs is a recent signee, expectations for him were modest—he only received the playbook a few days ago. Sure, Altmyer is an undrafted rookie, but a great performance could have solidified him as the guy to beat. Now, entering the next preseason game, Dobbs will have another week of practice under his belt to familiarize himself with the offense, meaning Altmyer will have lost his advantage over the veteran. At this point, I think both quarterbacks will be on equal footing, and this battle could shift on a weekly basis. Altmyer can still win this job, but he came up a bit short in his first opportunity. Miles Frazier, OL Entering this week, Frazier was an unquestioned roster lock in my eyes. However, his performance against the Bengals made me think twice about how safe his roster spot truly is—if it was at 99 percent before, my confidence now might be somewhere around 90 percent, as in still a good bet to make the roster but perhaps worthy of including on Bubble Watch next week. Frazier was dinged for three holding penalties in the game, a frustrating showing for the young lineman. In his first game of 2025, Frazier was penalized twice for false starts, only seeing a handful of snaps the rest of the season. Is it still a recurring trend, or is his small sample size skewing the results? Only time will tell. As a guard with the first team, Frazier was fine, though he was overshadowed by the likes of Christian Mahogany and Blake Miller. Later in the game, he subbed in at left tackle, flexing his positional versatility. However, he also showcased his rawness, getting beat badly on a sack. I think his ability to play across the offensive line makes him valuable, but we need to see some good offensive line play—after all, it doesn’t matter if you play every spot poorly. Payton Turner, DE I would normally argue that it isn’t fair to ding a player for not playing in a game, but the clock is ticking for Turner to show that he deserves a roster spot—he needs these snaps. Working against the injured Turner is that the front seven played fairly well against the Bengals, meaning a fair number of defensive linemen competing for his roster spot got a stock-up on Thursday. Ahmed Hassanein, perhaps his biggest competition, was outstanding. Eric O’Neill stood out often. Skyler Gill-Howard looked formidable as a pass rusher. Chris Smith and Myles Adams had some nice run stuffs. Even the likes of Ben Stille and Anthony Lucas had some moments. The fact remains that the Lions have a lot of roster-worthy players along their defensive line, yet very few roster spots are available. Turner needs to get on the field soon, or else he will get outpaced by his competition as they put up good tape.
author: John Whiticar

title: 13 winners, 6 losers from Detroit Lions preseason game vs. Bengals
summary: The Detroit Lions fell to the Cincinnati Bengals on the road, 16-14, to open the exhibition portion of the schedule in Dan Campbell’s sixth season at the helm. Despite a slopfest from a weather, turnover, and penalty standpoint, there were still plenty of beneficial aspects to the competitive faceoff between the two feline teams at […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OHIO - AUGUST 13: Josh Johnson #11 of the Cincinnati Bengals runs the ball against Skyler Gill-Howard #50 of the Detroit Lions during the second half of the preseason game at Paycor Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Cincinnati, Ohio. (Photo by Justin Casterline/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions fell to the Cincinnati Bengals on the road, 16-14, to open the exhibition portion of the schedule in Dan Campbell’s sixth season at the helm. Despite a slopfest from a weather, turnover, and penalty standpoint, there were still plenty of beneficial aspects to the competitive faceoff between the two feline teams at Paycor Stadium. Most notably, the preseason opener provided plenty of evaluation value. The Lions played arguably more players who are likely to make the 53-man roster than in any preseason game under Campbell, while several unproven and developing players received valuable repetitions against Bengals starters on both sides of the ball. Of course, it’s still preseason, and these evaluations shouldn’t carry more weight than what the Lions have shown throughout their first 11 training camp practices. But the game remains an important piece of the development and roster evaluation process. Some players further strengthened their cases for regular-season roles, while others were unable to capitalize on their opportunities and separate themselves from the competition. With that in mind, here are my winners and losers from the Lions’ preseason opener. Winner: DE Ahmed Hassanein One of the early breakout stars of Detroit Lions training camp, Ahmed Hassanein has transformed both his game and his body from a year ago. He’s gone from a player I wasn’t sure would make the 53-man roster to someone who might not even need to play in the Lions’ third preseason game against the Colts—and could potentially carve out an early-season gameday role. It’s been close to the best possible two-week surge Hassanein could have hoped for to begin training camp. It’s difficult for a defensive lineman to fill up the box score as triumphantly as Hassanein did in a preseason game, particularly a reserve who started his damage by sacking Joe Burrow against Cincinnati’s starting offensive line. Hassanein finished with four tackles, three quarterback hits, 2.0 sacks, two tackles for loss, and a forced fumble. His red-zone sack and forced fumble of Josh Johnson was another reassuring example of his ability to shut down a drive while creating a takeaway opportunity. After 29 highly productive snaps against the Bengals, the enigmatic edge rusher continues to exceed expectations. Winner: DT Skyler Gill-Howard Another young defensive lineman whose arrow continues pointing up, Skyler Gill-Howard checked another box Thursday night by consistently finding himself around the football. Gill-Howard only recorded one tackle, but he did so by traversing frequent-flier-miles fiend Josh Johnson. Gill-Howard galloped after the quarterback on third down, eventually chasing him down short of the sticks and forcing Cincinnati to settle for a field goal. It was an impressive display of both effort and athleticism. Gill-Howard had already crumbled Johnson earlier with a quarterback hit that forced an incompletion, aided by Anthony Lucas screaming off the edge and flushing Johnson from the pocket. Gill-Howard later added a second quarterback hit with an inside fake into a swim move that left second-year Bengals guard Jalen Rivers looking about as useful as a mop without a bucket. Gill-Howard told Pride of Detroit after Practice No. 9 that things were beginning to click for him as a pass rusher. That progress was evident Thursday night. Loser: WR Isaac TeSlaa The spring shine has certainly worn off for Isaac TeSlaa. On the heels of an already quiet and complicated training camp, it would have been difficult to script a more detrimental preseason debut. Several players battling for the WR5 role made a play or two at the catch point or with the ball in their hands on passes from Luke Altmeyer and Josh Dobbs. Meanwhile, the Lions’ hopeful WR3 did just about the opposite of playmaking. TeSlaa coughed up his first target off his helmet, resulting in an interception. Two drives later, he had another opportunity to respond but dropped a well-thrown slant on fourth down to end the possession. Questions may now begin to creep in about how much the Lions can trust TeSlaa with primary WR3 snaps in Week 1 against a Brandon Staley-led defense, particularly for an offense already preparing to start a new backup center in a big spot. Winner: RB Jacob Saylors With Isiah Pacheco, Sione Vaki, and his closest RB4 competition, Jabari Small, all shelved, Jacob set sail on an expedition to show Lions coaches he can be a potent part of the offense, as Dan Campbell called it postgame, while strengthening his case for a roster spot. Saylors finished the evening with eight carries for 55 yards (6.9 yards per carry), including a long of 27 yards and four other runs of seven or more yards. He also added three catches for 28 receiving yards. Beyond the production, Saylors showed intimidating acceleration and consistently ran through arm tackles while also proving competent in pass protection and as a receiving threat out of the backfield. Saylors not only looked noticeably fresher than he did last season, when he arrived in Detroit directly off a UFL season, but also like a player poised to surpass the two offensive touches he received for the Lions last year. Winner: LG Christian Mahogany On the back end of Saylors’ strong performance was the blocking of Christian Mahogany. While he had his share of mishaps with penalties and a miscommunication on a blitz pickup, Mahogany was road-grading up front and helped provide multiple sparks in the run game. When Saylors was motoring into the second level, more often than not Mahogany played a part by creating vertical displacement at the line of scrimmage in both zone and gap-scheme concepts. Mahogany was pushing some serious plates from the start, helping spring Saylors’ first carry for seven yards by plowing Dexter Lawrence downfield. Beyond showcasing his power in the run game, Mahogany also benefited from 24 live reps in pass protection after entering training camp delayed by injury and going through a slow ramp-up period. With Mahogany now the healthiest among himself, Ben Bartch, and Juice Scruggs—and Scruggs potentially needed at center—Thursday’s performance gives Mahogany an early lead in the position battle for the honor of lining up next to left tackle Penei Sewell. Loser: CB Ennis Rakestraw Rakestraw received some positive limelight from the Lions TV broadcast, including more background on his story, but aside from forcing one early incompletion, his performance was close to the defensive equivalent of Isaac TeSlaa’s evening—if not worse. For a much-maligned high draft pick who has yet to fully put it together and has naysayers questioning some of Brad Holmes’ decisions, Thursday was close to a worst-case scenario. Rakestraw was targeted early and often. It wasn’t just Ja’Marr Chase doing the damage, either, as Rakestraw surrendered chain-moving completions to Andrei Iosivas and Kolbie Young as well. The unfortunate cherry on top was Rakestraw exiting the game due to injury. Luckily, the injury isn’t serious, and he’ll still have opportunities in practice and the preseason to show growth and make his case for snaps deeper in the cornerback pecking order this season. Quick Hitters Winners: RT Blake Miller — There were still a few snaps where Miller was caught lunging or stopping his feet, but overall it was a promising first performance in a Lions uniform. He received plenty of valuable reps against Myles Murphy, Cedric Johnson, and Jonathan Allen. ED Eric O’Neill — Showed a lot more bounce and spring in his step, beating Zeus Jr. for a quarterback hit on Joe Burrow on third down to force a field goal. O’Neill added a handful of impressive pass-rush wins and…

title: Green Bay Packers Depth Chart: What Week 1 of the preseason taught us
summary: We’re here today to take our best stab at what the Green Bay Packers think of their current roster. Yes, there’s an open roster spot on the team right now, so there are only 90 players listed on this depth chart, not the typical 91. We don’t know what’s happening behind closed doors, be it […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MN - JANUARY 04: Green Bay Packers defensive end Karl Brooks (94) looks on during the second half of the NFL game between the Green Bay Packers and Minnesota Vikings on January 4th, 2026, at U.S. Bank Stadium in Minneapolis, MN. (Photo by Bailey Hillesheim/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images We’re here today to take our best stab at what the Green Bay Packers think of their current roster. Yes, there’s an open roster spot on the team right now, so there are only 90 players listed on this depth chart, not the typical 91. We don’t know what’s happening behind closed doors, be it practices that weren’t open to the public or how players are picking up the playbook and taking meeting lessons onto the field. Even in open practices, the media can’t have their eyes on every player at all times. This is all to say: The club knows more about these players than we do. What we do know, though, is how the Packers’ depth chart has played out in the past. We also just learned a little more information about how the team thinks of their newer players, as they showed their hand a bit with how they deployed their positional rotations in their preseason opener against the Pittsburgh Steelers. With that in mind, here is the pecking order at each position, including every player on the team, after charting the Packers’ rotations with their first- and second-team units and comparing those numbers to the overall snap counts from the game . Quarterback Jordan Love Tyrod Taylor Kyle McCord With the release of Kyron Drones , the pecking order in Green Bay is Jordan Love, Tyrod Taylor and then Kyle McCord, though I’m sure some want to see McCord get more time with the second-team offense after he posted a 91.1 rating against the Pittsburgh Steelers. Running Back Josh Jacobs (groin) MarShawn Lloyd Chris Brooks (hamstring) Pierre Strong Jr. Jaden Nixon Damien Martinez Neither Josh Jacobs nor Chris Brooks played against Pittsburgh, but MarShawn Lloyd played all first-team offensive snaps and received the first snaps with the second team. Pierre Strong Jr. out-snapped UDFA rookie Jaden Nixon 7-to-3, while Damien Martinez only worked with the third- and fourth-team offenses. Receiver Christian Watson Matthew Golden Jayden Reed Savion Williams Bo Melton Skyy Moore Isaiah Neyor J. Michael Sturdivant Will Sheppard Kaden Prather Kisean Johnson Chris Hilton Jr. To no one’s surprise, the number one offense featured Christian Watson and Matthew Golden on the outside and Jayden Reed in the slot. The only receiver who got in the mix, other than those three, was Savion Williams for one rep. For shorthand: Think of Williams as Watson’s backup, Bo Melton as Golden’s backup and Skyy Moore as Reed’s backup. That’s how they used these players. Melton, Williams and Moore all got at least nine snaps with the second-team offense, while Isaiah Neyor got four. Neyor played 37 total offensive snaps versus Pittsburgh to J. Michael Sturdivant’s 26 and Will Sheppard’s 16. Kaden Prather, Kisean Johnson and Chris Hilton Jr., who were all added to the Packers’ roster recently, had no more than seven offensive snaps in the game. Tight End Tucker Kraft (knee) Luke Musgrave (PUP, neck) Josh Whyle Drake Dabney Messiah Swinson McCallan Castles Thomas Yassmin With both of the Packers’ top tight ends out with injuries, Drake Dabney got the “start” at tight end, but he was out-snapped 8-to-3 by Josh Whyle with the first-team offense. On the second team, Dabney played 11 snaps to Messiah Swinson’s 5. McCallan Castles and Thomas Yassmin, Green Bay’s international exemption player, each played six offensive snaps, but Castles also played 11 special teams reps to Yassmin’s 3. Castles had a big tackle on special teams, if you’re into that thing. Offensive Line Zach Bako-Bewele (RT, knee) Jordan Morgan (LT) Sean Rhyan (C) Anthony Belton (RG/RT) Aaron Banks (LG, knee) Jacob Monk (G/C) Jager Burton (G/C) Donovan Jennings (G/C) Darian Kinnard (RT/G) John Williams (LT/G/C) Dillon Wade (G) Travis Glover (T) Josh Gesky (G) Dylan Barrett (G) Dalton Cooper (T) Brant Banks (T) Zach Bako-Bewele and Aaron Banks both were held out of action versus the Steelers, which led the Packers to roll with a starting offensive line of Jordan Morgan, Jager Burton, Sean Rhyan, Jacob Monk and Anthony Belton (left to right). Rhyan was pulled out of the game when the second-team offense played, while the other “starters” remained in the game. Monk slid into center for Rhyan, which allowed Donovan Jennings to play right guard with the second-team unit. Later in the game, Darian Kinnard (8 snaps, injured), John Williams (32), Dillon Wade (24), Travis Glover (18), Josh Gesky (16), Dylan Barrett (6), Dalton Cooper (6) and Brant Banks (6) played with the third- and fourth-team offenses, coming into the game in that order. Defensive Line Devonte Wyatt (knee) Javon Hargrave (knee) Karl Brooks Warren Brinson Chris McClellan Jordon Riley (PUP, ankle) Anthony Campbell Nazir Stackhouse Jonathan Ford Jaden Crumedy Green Bay’s top two defensive linemen continue to recover from knee injuries, but it is worth noting that Karl Brooks was treated like a premier starter, as he only got time with the first-team unit. The only other players who only played with first-teamers against the Steelers were: quarterback Jordan Love, receiver Christian Watson, receiver Matthew Golden, receiver Jayden Reed, center Sean Rhyan, edge defender Lukas Van Ness, edge defender Barryn Sorrell, linebacker Zaire Franklin, linebacker Edgerrin Cooper, safety Xavier McKinney and safety Evan Williams. At this point, I’m thinking that Brooks is going to be starting in the Packers’ 3-4 base defense in Week 1, which means that Javon Hargrave will likely be playing nose tackle in those looks. With the first- and second-team defenses, Warren Brinson played 16 snaps, Chris McClellan played 11 snaps, Anthony Campbell and Nazir Stackhouse each played 10 snaps and Jonathan Ford played 8 snaps. Ford, notably, played almost exclusively as an odd-front nose tackle head-up on the center, while the rest of the defensive linemen moved around. He has the most defined role of the Packers’ backup linemen. Jordon Riley is likely to miss the entire 2026 season as he recovers from his Achilles tendon tear. Jaden Crumedy is clearly last in the pecking order in Green Bay, while the final roster spot (sixth defensive tackle) on the 53-man roster should be highly competitive, with Campbell, Stackhouse and Ford each showing flashes from time to time. Edge Rusher Micah Parsons (PUP, knee) Lukas Van Ness Barryn Sorrell Brenton Cox Jr. Collin Oliver Dani Dennis-Sutton (illness) Nyjalik Kelly Arron Mosby As mentioned before, both Lukas Van Ness and Barryn Sorrell were treated like entrenched starters by the Packers. Brenton Cox Jr. played 14 snaps with the first- and second-team defenses, while Collin Oliver played 12, Nyjalik Kelly played 10 and Arron Mosby played 8. Whenever Dani Dennis-Sutton returns to the field from his illness, he will likely cut into Kelly and Mosby’s playing time, considering that Kelly didn’t play his responsibilities well and Mosby is primarily a special teamer. Micah Parsons is not expected to be activated from the PUP list until at least Week 5, the first opportunity that NFL teams can call up players to the active roster if they start the regular season on the physically unable to perform list. Linebacker Zaire Franklin Edgerrin Cooper Isaiah McDuffie Ty’Ron Hopper Nick Niemann Kristian Welch T.J. Quinn Zaire Franklin is the team’s starting Mike linebacker, and Isaiah McDuffie is his backup. Edgerrin Cooper is the starting Will linebacker, and Ty’Ron Hopper is his backup. Nick Niemann will likely make the team as a special teams ace. Kristian Welch and T.J. Quinn each played 30 snaps on defense on Thursday, but Welch, another big-time special teams contributor, outsnapped Quinn 19-to-8 in the kicking game. Welch will probably be a practice…

title: Packers clear the runway for Kyle McCord to be QB3
summary: On Saturday, just two days after the Green Bay Packers’ preseason opener, the Packers announced that they have parted ways with quarterback Kyron Drones, who was originally signed by the team as an undrafted free agent immediately following the 2026 NFL draft. Drones signed with Green Bay for just $5,000 in guarantees, which ranked 10th […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - AUGUST 13: Kyle McCord #18 of the Green Bay Packers looks to pass during the third quarter against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Acrisure Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Joe Sargent/Getty Images) | Getty Images On Saturday, just two days after the Green Bay Packers’ preseason opener, the Packers announced that they have parted ways with quarterback Kyron Drones, who was originally signed by the team as an undrafted free agent immediately following the 2026 NFL draft. Drones signed with Green Bay for just $5,000 in guarantees, which ranked 10th among 12 UDFA signings at the quarterback position this offseason . Head coach Matt LaFleur has said in the past that it’s difficult to rep four quarterbacks in practice, and that his preference is that he holds onto three. So with that in mind, it shouldn’t be shocking that Drones was released after his one-pass attempt (an incompletion) and three-sack performance in the fourth quarter against the Pittsburgh Steelers. Notably, one of those sacks came on a screen where Drones just never let go of the ball. One of them was a screen btw pic.twitter.com/iCAhGDs1oo — Justis Mosqueda (@JuMosq) August 14, 2026 With Drones out of the picture in the quarterback room, it seems clear that the Packers will roll with Tyrod Taylor (as the backup) and Kyle McCord (likely as a practice squadder) moving forward. Green Bay played their starters for just one drive in Week 1 of the preseason, so expect to see a lot more of Taylor and McCord in upcoming preseason games. McCord was picked up by the Packers as a reserve-futures signing (typically the deals that practice squaders sign to be retained on the offseason roster) back in January. As a rookie sixth-round pick last year, he spent the entire season on the Philadelphia Eagles’ practice squad. Last preseason, McCord went 24 of 56 for 191 yards, one touchdown and two interceptions with the Eagles. McCord was 12 of 16 for 102 yards and a 91.1 passer rating in Green Bay’s loss to Pittsburgh in the 2026 preseason opener. He led the team in every major passing statistic, other than sacks and sack yardage — which was held by Drones. On Friday, LaFleur said that the Packers didn’t suffer any long-term injuries during their Week 1 preseason game, which means that offensive lineman Darian Kinnard and defensive lineman Anthony Campbell should be fine moving forward. Green Bay now has an open roster spot on its 91-man offseason roster, but it’s unclear which direction they will take. Recently, they’ve been working out tight ends, receivers and safeties, but they’ve also signed players at those positions already. The Packers signed safeties Trey Dean III and Tra Fluellen on August 11th, claimed receiver Chris Hilton Jr. on August 10th, signed receiver Kisean Johnson on August 9th and signed tight ends McCallan Castles and Drew Biber (who has already been released) on August 4th. They also signed receiver Kaden Prather on July 31st and tight end Thomas Yassmin, the team’s international exemption player, on July 28th.
author: Justis Mosqueda

title: Here’s who played for the Packers’ 1st- and 2nd-team units in the preseason opener
summary: The Green Bay Packers’ snap counts from their preseason opener against the Pittsburgh Steelers dropped yesterday, but they don’t tell you very much. When players like cornerback Jaylin Simpson are leading the team in total snaps, it doesn’t really paint a clear picture of who is getting in the mix with the Packers’ first- and […]
full_text: DENVER, CO - AUGUST 18: Jonathan Ford #99 of the Green Bay Packers walks along the field during an NFL football game against the Denver Broncos at Empower Field at Mile High on August 18, 2024 in Denver, CO. (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers’ snap counts from their preseason opener against the Pittsburgh Steelers dropped yesterday, but they don’t tell you very much. When players like cornerback Jaylin Simpson are leading the team in total snaps, it doesn’t really paint a clear picture of who is getting in the mix with the Packers’ first- and second-team units. So as a gift to you, I have charted all of the Packers’ first- and second-team snaps against the Steelers, on both the offensive and defensive sides of the ball. This gives us a better look at what Green Bay’s depth chart looks like right now, compared to raw snap counts. I hope you enjoy (and I’ll be doing this moving forward in the preseason, too). I’ also added some notes when I thought they were relevant. Packers 1st Team Offense Quarterback Jordan Love: 9 snaps Running Back MarShawn Lloyd: 9 snaps Reminder: Josh Jacobs (groin) and Chris Brooks (hamstring) were both held out of the game with injuries. Receiver Matthew Golden: 9 snaps Christian Watson: 8 snaps Jayden Reed: 7 snaps Savion Williams: 1 snap As expected, Jayden Reed only got on the field in three-receiver sets, as he’s been used almost exclusively as a slot receiver in his time with Green Bay . That doesn’t seem to be changing in 2026. Savion Williams got in for one snap when Christian Watson needed a breather. Tight End Josh Whyle: 8 snaps Drake Dabney: 3 snaps While Drake Dabney “started” the game and Josh Whyle didn’t, Whyle out-snapped Dabney with the first-team unit. Generally, Dabney played an in-line position more than Whyle did on Thursday night. Reminder: Tucker Kraft (knee) and Luke Musgrave (neck) were held out of action. Offensive Line Jordan Morgan: 9 snaps (LT) Jager Burton: 9 snaps (LG) Sean Rhyan: 9 snaps (C) Jacob Monk: 9 snaps (RG) Anthony Belton: 9 snaps (RT) Without expected starting left guard Aaron Banks (knee) and starting right tackle Zach Bako-Bewele (knee), Jager Burton and Jacob Monk entered the starting lineup. Monk actually played right guard, pushing expected starting right guard Anthony Belton to right tackle, as the Packers don’t have much tackle depth at the moment. Packers 2nd Team Offense Quarterback Tyrod Taylor: 13 snaps Running Back Pierre Strong Jr.: 7 snaps MarShawn Lloyd: 3 snaps Jaden Nixon: 3 snaps With Lloyd getting all of the work with the first-team unit, Pierre Strong Jr. got the most burn with the second stringers. Notably, undrafted rookie Jaden Nixon got looks ahead of Damien Martinez, a 2025 draft pick who the Packers picked up in December. Receiver Bo Melton: 11 snaps Savion Williams: 11 snaps Skyy Moore: 9 snaps Isaiah Neyor: 4 snaps Bo Melton and Savion Williams were the “starting” outside receivers for the second-team unit, with Skyy Moore playing the role of Jayden Reed — a player who only came onto the field in three-receiver sets, mostly as a slot receiver. Isaiah Neyor got in the mix, but only when Melton and Williams were subbed out for a breather. Tight End Drake Dabney: 11 snaps Messiah Swinson: 5 snaps Dabney got the most looks at tight end with the second-team unit, and apparently Messiah Swinson is the next man up, ahead of McCallan Castles and international exemption Thomas Yassmin, whose first practice with Green Bay was on Family Night. Offensive Line Jordan Morgan: 13 snaps (LT) Jager Burton: 13 snaps (LG) Jacob Monk: 13 snaps (C) Donovan Jennings: 13 snaps (RG) Anthony Belton: 13 snaps (RT) Morgan, Burton, Monk and Belton stayed on the field with the second-team unit, but Monk moved to center as Sean Rhyan was shut down for the day. This opened up a spot at right guard for Donovan Jennings to jump into the lineup. Yes, they all got looks ahead of the likes of Darian Kinnard, John Williams and Travis Glover. Packers 1st Team Defense Defensive Line Karl Brooks: 3 snaps Warren Brinson: 2 snaps Jonathan Ford: 1 snap Both Devonte Wyatt (knee) and Javon Hargrave (knee), the Packers’ most important defensive linemen, weren’t dressed up for the game on Thursday. Jonathan Ford’s snap with the first-team unit came as a 3-4 nose tackle (more on this later), while Karl Brooks and Brinson were the “ends” in that look. Brooks and Brinson also played the nickel snap before the Packers’ first-team defense’s final play: a subpackage where edge rusher Lukas Van Ness kicked into the interior. Brooks was the lone defensive lineman on the field for that rush package. Edge Defender Lukas Van Ness: 3 snaps Barryn Sorrell: 3 snaps Collin Oliver: 1 snap Lukas Van Ness and Barryn Sorrell were the starting edges in this game, and they didn’t get any work after the first-team defense’s three-play drive. Collin Oliver got in the game as a subpackage rusher when Van Ness kicked inside, ahead of Brenton Cox Jr. It’s worth mentioning here that Dani Dennis-Sutton, the Packers’ fourth-round rookie, missed the game with an illness. Off-Ball Linebacker Zaire Franklin: 3 snaps Edgerrin Cooper: 3 snaps Cornerback Keisean Nixon: 3 snaps Brandon Cisse: 3 snaps Safety Xavier McKinney: 3 snaps Evan Williams: 3 snaps Kitan Oladapo: 2 snaps Kitan Oladapo got two snaps with the first-team defense, both in the slot as an injury replacement for Javon Bullard (foot). Packers 2nd Team Defense Defensive Line Warren Brinson: 14 snaps Chris McClellan: 11 snaps Anthony Campbell: 10 snaps Nazir Stackhouse: 10 snaps Jonathan Ford: 7 snaps Jaden Crumedy: 1 snap Again, Ford was used almost exclusively as an odd front nose tackle with the second-team defense, while the rest of the linemen moved around. It seems like the team has a defined role for Ford, unlike the rest of their group — including the big-bodied Nazir Stackhouse. Edge Defender Brenton Cox Jr.: 14 snaps Collin Oliver: 12 snaps Nyjalik Kelly: 10 snaps Arron Mosby: 8 snaps Cox outsnapped Oliver with the second-team unit, even though Oliver got in with the first-team unit in the pressure package. I’m guessing that Nyjalik Kelly and Arron Mosby will get fewer opportunities with the second-team unit when Dennis-Sutton returns to the field. Kelly struggled playing assignment football throughout the night . Off-Ball Linebacker Isaiah McDuffie: 22 snaps Ty’Ron Hopper: 19 snaps The three snaps that Ty’Ron Hopper didn’t play while Isaiah McDuffie was on the field came when Jonathan Gannon called one-linebacker “Penny” packages . Cornerback Keisean Nixon: 17 snaps Brandon Cisse: 17 snaps Benjamin St-Juste: 5 snaps Jaylin Simpson: 5 snaps Keisean Nixon and Brandon Cisse, who played the first-team snaps at outside cornerback, played the first 17 snaps of the second-team defense, too. When they were shut down is when Benjamin St-Juste and Jaylin Simpson got their shot at playing outside cornerback with the second-team unit. All of Simpson’s snaps here came at outside cornerback. He did end up playing some slot reps with the third- and fourth-string defenses later in the game, though. Quick reminder: Carrington Valentine was out with a hamstring and is battling with Cisse and St-Juste for the starting job opposite Nixon. Safety Kitan Oladapo: 22 snaps Mark Perry: 22 snaps Murvin Kenion III: 16 snaps In base 3-4 defense looks, the safeties were Kitan Oladapo and Mary Perry on the second-team defense. When the team played nickel packages, with five defensive backs on the field, Oladapo kicked into the slot, and Murvin Kenion III came off the bench to play safety. Oladapo looked a lot better as a true safety than he did when he was in the slot on Thursday.

title: Colts work out handful of players, including three veteran wideouts
summary: The Indianapolis Colts worked out a handful of veteran players on Saturday: quarterback Mark Gronowski, cornerback Jaylon Guilbeau, wide receiver Josh Reynolds, wide receiver Tre’Quan Smith, and wide receiver Equanimeous St. Brown. The 6’2”, 226 pound Gronowski was signed as an undrafted rookie free agent by the Miami Dolphins earlier this offseason, but was waived […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CA - JULY 24: San Francisco 49ers wide receiver Equanimeous St. Brown (7) adjusts his helmet during San Francisco 49ers Training Camp on July 24, 2025 at the SAP Performance Facility in Santa Clara, CA. (Photo by Matthew Huang/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Indianapolis Colts worked out a handful of veteran players on Saturday: quarterback Mark Gronowski, cornerback Jaylon Guilbeau, wide receiver Josh Reynolds, wide receiver Tre’Quan Smith, and wide receiver Equanimeous St. Brown. The 6’2”, 226 pound Gronowski was signed as an undrafted rookie free agent by the Miami Dolphins earlier this offseason, but was waived in early August. He was a 2x FCS National Champion, 2x FCS Championship Game MVP, FCS First-Team All-American, and 2x MVFC Offensive Player of the Year previously with South Dakota St. He started last season for the Iowa Hawkeyes, completing 166 of 262 pass attempts (63.4%) for 1,741 passing yards, 10 passing touchdowns, and 7 interceptions during 13 starts. He was the 2026 Offensive MVP of this year’s earlier East-West Shrine game. Meanwhile, Jaylon Guilbeau is a 5,11”, 190 pound cornerback who was signed by the Carolina Panthers as an undrafted rookie free agent following the 2026 NFL Draft. He had been placed on the reserve/non-football injury list, but was subsequently waived. He had 40 tackles (22 solo), a sack, an interception and 3 passes defensed during 12 starts as a senior cornerback for the Texas Longhorns defense this past season. Then there’s Josh Reynolds, as the former 2017 4th round pick of the Los Angeles Rams, who’s also played for the Tennessee Titans, Detroit Lions, Denver Broncos, Jacksonville Jaguars, and New York Jets. The 6,3”, 192 pound wideout has 244 receptions for 3,228 total receiving yards (13.2 ypr. avg.) and 20 touchdown receptions during 121 career games (58 starts). Next here, is Tre’Quan Smith, who’s a former 2018 3rd round pick of the New Orleans Saints that’s also played for the Denver Broncos and Detroit Lions organization. The 6,2”, 210 pound wideout 131 receptions for 1,764 total receiving yards (13.5 ypr. avg.) and 18 touchdown receptions during 67 career games (35 starts). Lastly, Equanimeous St. Brown is a 2018 6th round pick of the Green Bay Packers, who’s also played for the Chicago Bears, New Orleans Saints, and San Francisco 49ers. The 6,5”, 214 pound wideout has 63 receptions for 928 total receiving yards (14.7 ypr. avg.) and 2 touchdown receptions during 62 career games (28 starts).
author: Luke Schultheis

title: Colts Training Camp ‘Day 11’: Quick Hits
summary: Following a Thursday night preseason opener tie, the Indianapolis Colts were back in action indoors during otherwise a soggy late Saturday afternoon—for what was a rather uneventful training camp practice, with the team primarily focusing on end zone work. I was actually able to attend this one as a credentialed member of the media, so […]
full_text: WESTFIELD, IN - JULY 31: Indianapolis Colts cornerback Justin Walley (27) runs through a drill during the Indianapolis Colts training camp practice on July 31, 2025 at the Grand Park Sports Campus in Westfield, IN. (Photo by Zach Bolinger/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Following a Thursday night preseason opener tie, the Indianapolis Colts were back in action indoors during otherwise a soggy late Saturday afternoon—for what was a rather uneventful training camp practice, with the team primarily focusing on end zone work. I was actually able to attend this one as a credentialed member of the media, so I’ll change the format up a bit: Colts Stingy Secondary Wins Afternoon For another training camp practice, it looked like the Colts secondary got the better of the Indianapolis wide receivers, especially with Alec Pierce still out (who we’ll get to in a bit here). That seems to have been a common theme so far this training camp, and when the trio of Sauce Gardner, Charvarius Ward, and Justin Walley are all fully healthy, the Colts project to have one of the best cornerback rooms atop their depth chart in the entire league. In particular, starting cornerback Justin Walley, who was playing on the outside in place of Ward in this one, had at least a few deflections of note. Oftentimes, Jones was forced to hold the football in the passing pocket until a Colts receiver could finally free up from tight coverage. That may not happen in a real game, where the pass rush will get to him a lot quicker and not let up, likely seeing more ‘coverage sacks.’ That being said, while the Colts secondary did stifle Jones for much of the afternoon, he connected on at least a few touchdowns passes in 11-on-11 red zone work, including to Josh Downs, who came up gingerly after the acrobatic touchdown catch but was able to walk off the field and be attended to by trainers. Downs did later return to practice. Ashton Dulin, Seth McGowan, Laquon Treadwell, and Tyler Warren, who also had an acrobatic dandy, caught the other touchdown receptions from Jones on the afternoon from what I saw. Both backup quarterbacks Anthony Richardson and Riley Leonard were up-and-down in their own end zone work, but each showed impressive chemistry with Colts wideout Raylen Sharpe, who caught a handful of receiving touchdowns on the afternoon during red zone work from the pair of backup passers. Colts running back Ulysses Bentley IV also stood out, having made a few nice catches on the afternoon. He continues to have a strong camp and may not be just a player purely practice squad bound as it stands. From a pass rushing standpoint, 3rd-year edge Laiatu Latu was very active again, recording maybe 2.0 would be sacks that I saw, as well as a handful of other QB pressures on Jones. Increasingly Out of Commission Colts Some of it may be some rest for the Colts players who just played on Thursday night, but among the players who did not practice today: linebacker CJ Allen (hamstring), offensive guard Jalen Farmer, wide receiver Anthony Gould, running back DJ Giddens (hamstring), defensive tackle Derrick Nnadi, wide receiver Alec Pierce (ankle/PUP), offensive tackle Nolan Rucci, offensive tackle Luke Tenuta (knee), and cornerback Charvarius Ward (back) Pierce Doing Light Work Along Sidelines Speaking of Pierce, the Colts’ lucratively re-signed leading wideout from last season was doing light work along with sidelines with Colts wide receivers coach Reggie Wayne during part of Saturday’s training camp practice. Pierce still wasn’t jogging or cutting on the ankle, but he was stationary, catching passes from Wayne. It wasn’t just a simple ‘pitch-and-catch’ game though, as Pierce was having to move and contort his body to make acrobatic, athletic catches. Brian Mason Already Back Colts special teams coordinator Brian Mason, who tore multiple ligaments in his left knee at the end of Thursday night’s game after a sideline collision with players, was already back on the field with a knee brace. One special teams item of note was that rookie edge Caden Curry was among the Colts players who took some long snapping reps, likely as emergency options in case long snapper Luke Rhodes were ever to get hurt in a game and be unable to return to the football field. The Colts are rightfully making emergency contingency plans.
author: Luke Schultheis

title: DeForest Buckner is healthy and boy, do the Colts need him to be
summary: A behemoth of a man came racing over on an electric bike. Big 99, DeForest Buckner, had media availability at the end of Colts training camp on Saturday night. Things were moved inside due to weather, but Buckner was as sunny as could be. He was all smiles as he talked to the media and […]
full_text: WESTFIELD, IN - AUGUST 6: Indianapolis Colts defensive tackle DeForest Buckner (99) runs through a drill during the Indianapolis Colts training camp practice on August 6, 2026 at the Grand Park Sports Campus in Westfield, IN. (Photo by Zach Bolinger/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images A behemoth of a man came racing over on an electric bike. Big 99, DeForest Buckner, had media availability at the end of Colts training camp on Saturday night. Things were moved inside due to weather, but Buckner was as sunny as could be. He was all smiles as he talked to the media and described how he is back to feeling good which is music to Colts fans’ ears. This season wasn’t to be taken for granted by Buckner, and there was a solid chance it might not have even happened. After sustaining a herniated disc in his neck in Week 9 which caused him to lose feeling in his upper body, Buckner fought his way back into the lineup in a late matchup against the 49ers. It was short-lived as he endured season ending surgery. It was a disappointing season for a man who rarely missed any time over his career. Fast forward to the 2026 season, one that was up in the air, and Buckner is feeling back to his old self. He is a full participant in training camp, and while you might not see him in the preseason, he will be out there and ready Week 1. Once he got popped at practice and saw that he was ok, Buckner said it was all behind him at that point. The Colts better hope he is back to form because they struggled severely without him. The losing streak to end the season didn’t have Buckner’s absence alone to thank, but it certainly didn’t help. The defense is a much different beast with Buckner in the middle. DeForest Buckner’s size, ability, and leadership are crucial to the Colts’ success in 2026. Without him plugging up holes and taking on double teams, this defense will struggle. He has proven to be one of the most important and reliable pieces brought in outside of the draft. If Buckner is back to full strength, this defense will pose some problems for the rest of the NFL.
author: Jon Spradley

title: Colts receiving corps faces uncertainty as depth concerns linger on
summary: Westfield, Ind. — With the weather forcing the team to move Saturday’s training camp practice indoors, the Indianapolis Colts held a tight hour-long session at Droplight Grand Park Sports Campus focused primarily inside the red zone.  Starting quarterback Daniel Jones showcased his ability to recognize a different mix of coverages and deliver strong throws in […]
full_text: NASHVILLE, TENNESSEE - OCTOBER 13: Indianapolis Colts receiver Josh Downs #1 dives for extra yards against the Tennessee Titans in the fourth quarter at Nissan Stadium —October 13, 2024 in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Wesley Hitt/Getty Images) | Getty Images Westfield, Ind. — With the weather forcing the team to move Saturday’s training camp practice indoors, the Indianapolis Colts held a tight hour-long session at Droplight Grand Park Sports Campus focused primarily inside the red zone. Starting quarterback Daniel Jones showcased his ability to recognize a different mix of coverages and deliver strong throws in closed space. Jones noticed the defense sitting underneath and split the coverage with a dart to tight end Tyler Warren on a wheel route for a 20-yard touchdown. that’s a Tyler touchdown pic.twitter.com/b9a9YZsJLm — Indianapolis Colts (@Colts) August 15, 2026 Jones later added some nice touch to toss a dime toward the far pylon for receiver Josh Downs, who made a leaping grab over cornerback Justin Walley for a 10-yard touchdown catch. Downs came down hard to make the sensational catch and briefly left the field to jog off some tightness in his right hamstring, but he later returned for the final team period and caught a short hitch on his first play back on the field. Jones was able to create plays while rolling out in space, too. Jones faked the play action, rolled right, released the throw while on the move and placed it just behind receiver Laquon Treadwell, who adjusted to the pass thrown near his hip and held on for a 10-yard touchdown in tight coverage. Jones finished the practice completing 7-of-14 passes, with a few incompletions on plays where he willingly decided it was best to throw the ball away rather than force a pass. The lone mistake nearly resulted in a turnover when rookie linebacker Bryce Boettcher got a hand on one of Jones’ throws for what could have been a error near the goal line. Jones stationoed himself in the pocket and allowed the plays to develop, evidenced best on his final throw that was caught by Ashton Dulin in the end zone. The second-string quarterback competition kept reps split between Anthony Richardson Sr. and Riley Leonard as both passers had just five completions in team drills during the short practice. Richardson delivered a frozen rope on a comeback route to tight end Will Mallory toward the far pylon for a 10-yard touchdown, then he later connected with receiver Raylen Sharpe on a slant and a corner route in the final team drill. Leonard also found the end zone playing on a short field, connecting with Sharpe on a quick out and rookie Deion Burks on a drag route. The Colts’ wide receiver situation remains an volatile storyline with the season opener just four weeks away. Receiver Alec Pierce, who signed a four-year $114 million deal in March, has missed all 10 training camp practices while recovering from offseason ankle surgery, which leaves the Colts with limited depth outside the numbers. There are three receivers vying for the open WR3 spot right now, including Nick Westbrook-Ikhene, along with Dulin and Treadwell. Indy will choose to keep a handful of weapons, but with only one football, even the WR3 will have to make the most of any opportunities that present themselves. The Colts deploy plenty of 12 personnel with two tight end sets, so whoever emerges as the starter will still be limited to their role in the offense. There were also over a dozen receivers who participated Saturday, along with a trio of free agents who were brought in for workouts, Tre’Quan Smith, Josh Reynolds and Equanimeous St. Brown. Smith, a 2018 third-round pick, spent his first five seasons with the New Orleans Saints, but was limited to just 10 snaps with the Denver Broncos in 2023 and has not played since. Reynolds is still looking for a roster spot entering his tenth NFL season, but has become a journeyman while playing for five different organizations over the past five years. St. Brown was a 2018 sixth-round pick, but has appeared in only two games over the last two seasons, having last played for the Saints in 2024. The Colts have to navigate injuries on both sides of the ball. First-round draft pick C.J. Allen missed his fifth consecutive practice with a hamstring injury, which leaves even more doubt if he will be ready for Week 1. Akeem Davis-Gaither and Jaylon Carlies rotated with the starting linebackers Saturday as the depth chart continued to fill itself out. Cornerback Charvarius Ward was also out with back irritation, which allowed Cam Taylor-Britt to get most of the reps with the starters. Taylor-Britt was recently suspended for one game after violating the NFL’s personal-conduct policy, which stems from a legal case in Ohio where he pleaded guilty to reckless operation and driving without a license. The Colts will host three more practices at Grand Park, with Sunday’s practice scheduled for 4 p.m. Next week, the Colts host a pair of two-hour joint practices with the Atlanta Falcons to seal the final training camp in Westfield.
author: Thomas Butler-Guerrero

title: Caden Curry: Hometown Hero or Caesar Rayford 2.0?
summary: Center Grove High School alum Caden Curry made an enormous impact in his first appearance donning his hometown Indianapolis Colts’ horseshoe on an NFL field last Thursday. Appearing in the 2nd half of the opening preseason game against the New England Patriots, perhaps it was a childhood hatred of the rival Patriots from the Tom […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, IN - JUNE 11: Indianapolis Colts edge Caden Curry (55) runs through a drill during the Indianapolis Colts Minicamp on June 11, 2026 at the Indiana Farm Bureau Football Center in Indianapolis, IN. (Photo by Zach Bolinger/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Center Grove High School alum Caden Curry made an enormous impact in his first appearance donning his hometown Indianapolis Colts’ horseshoe on an NFL field last Thursday. Appearing in the 2nd half of the opening preseason game against the New England Patriots, perhaps it was a childhood hatred of the rival Patriots from the Tom Brady era that fueled his performance? Or could it be the pride in getting to suit up for his childhood team? Whether it was love or hate that provided the spark for his 6 Tackles (3 solo), 2 Tackles For Loss, 3 QB Hits, 1 Sack, 2 Pass Deflection night; Colts fans certainly can’t complain about his debut game. Colts EDGE Caden Curry in his Preseason Debut: 🔵 1.0 Sacks 🔵 4 QB Pressures 🔵 92.1 Pass Rush Grade 🔵 23.5% Win Rate @OhioStateFB pic.twitter.com/BmdqJBTWEB — PFF College (@PFF_College) August 14, 2026 Caden was able to stuff his stat sheet like a famous Hoosier pork tenderloin sandwich, spread out wider than you’d expect. He played along the line, inside as a 3 Technique (think DeForest Buckner’s spot) and outside as a Defensive End. He won as a pass rusher consistently, he won as a run stopper, and he even helped out in coverage by swatting 2 throws at the line of scrimmage. About as strong of a first look as you can find for a player. It certainly left an impression on Colts fans and media. . @Colts @CadenCurry14 who cares that he was the 214th pick out of @OhioStateFB … He showed up and showed out last night playing inside and outside. #BaldysBreakdowns pic.twitter.com/Gv4saR7NCi — Brian Baldinger (@BaldyNFL) August 14, 2026 This is extremely reactionary, but I’ve been thinking about it… Caden Curry is going to be a nightmare for opposing offenses. Ballard’s track record drafting edge rushers outside of Latu has been rough. He’s due to hit on an absolute stud. pic.twitter.com/g5klfu6wzK — SleeperColts (@SleeperColts) August 15, 2026 Caden Curry. Ballplayer. pic.twitter.com/sMR3NpinfB — Nate Tice (@Nate_Tice) August 14, 2026 I wasn't the biggest fan of Caden Curry as a true edge rusher prospect, but I was intrigued by some of his reps at 3-tech at Ohio State. Glad the Colts gave him some interior run on Thursday. 1 sack, 1 QB hit, and 2 PBU's rushing inside pic.twitter.com/TcHTFAaINn — Zach Hicks (@ZachHicks2) August 15, 2026 As touted as his performance was, is the hype train worthy of getting on to at this point? Myself and many others want to believe Curry is legit and will be a strong producer for the Colts. But there are some factors to consider before fully buying in this soon. Strength of opposing assignments Curry was being blocked by an Offensive Line consisting of James Hudson III, Mekhi Butler, JonDarius Morgan, Jacob Rizy, Dametrious Crownover by the time he entered the game. It isn’t crazy to say Curry faced better Offensive Linemen on a fair amount of assignments in the BIG10, as none of those players on the Patriots line were able to secure solid draft investment and the BIG10 is filled with powerhouse Offensive Line schools that regularly produce early round talent. With the scarcity of quality linemen in the NFL, the talent tiers between the best and worst linemen (and other tiers in the middle) can be stark. This dominance parallels the rise of another 1st year Edge Rusher from Colts history who dominated the preseason: Caesar Rayford in 2013. Is Caden Curry legit? Or is he Caesar Rayford 2.0 destroying backup OL? In 2013 Rayford, a free agent Edge from Arena Football recorded in the preseason: – 5 Sacks – 2 Forced Fumbles – 11 Tackles (7 Solo) He was traded to DAL for a conditional pick & recorded minimal stats https://t.co/aOOT90spsx pic.twitter.com/WEBWadV4DM — Jay Robins (@TheJayRobins) August 14, 2026 Rayford dominated the preseason, showcasing his 6’7 size and length along with nice burst to dominate the backup and practice squad offensive linemen of the NFL. The former Utah Blaze star for the Arena Football League generated a ton of hype from Colts media in this time. But then Colts General Manager Ryan Grigson traded him to the Cowboys around the time of roster cutdowns for a conditional pick. He racked up 5 tackles in 2013 but got injured and bounced around a few practice squads before leaving the NFL entirely in August 2015. On WTHR: Colts rookie Caesar Rayford ruling preseason http://t.co/fYjGW53pbZ — WTHR.com (@WTHRcom) August 20, 2013 Rayford should serve as a cautionary tale for fans to get too many expectations of late game heroics in preseason games. We already know Caden Curry can dominate against Linemen of a similar (if not better) talent and skill level than the Patriots 3rd string front based on Curry’s 2025 tape, which made him the highest graded DE in the Big10 last year. What we still don’t know , is how Curry would do consistently against the starting caliber linemen he will be asked to face in the NFL on a regular basis if he moves up the depth chart. Hopefully getting to play earlier in preseason games going forward will help answer that question. Low on the Colts Depth Chart With Caden Curry entering the game in the 2nd half and playing until the final snap of the game, it signaled that he still has a ways to go to rise up the Colts Defensive Line totem pole. Laiatu Latu, DeForest Buckner, and Grover Stewart are entrenched as 2026 starters. Arden Key, Jaylahn Tuimoloau, and Michael Clemons were in early on in the game, showing they will most likely make up the core group of Colts DE rotation at this point. Fellow rookie George Gumbs Jr also got snaps early on too, potentially indicating he could make the starting roster too. The #Colts have released their first depth chart of 2026. My thoughts on it: https://t.co/JLOmz9wpsS — Kevin Bowen (@KBowen1070) August 10, 2026 Curry did rotate to play 13 snaps inside at Defensive Tackle against the Patriots, but the DT room looks even more deep and tougher competition than the Edge spot. Behind the pair of 30+ year old starters, Adetomiwa Adebawore has shown growth as a situational pass rusher and gap shooter to warrant a strong rotational role. title: Clyde’s Colts recap
summary: Let me start by saying that I did not get the best look at the game. I got the Pat’s feed, so I heard too much McCourty twin banter, along with another guy who talked with a big Bob’s Discount Furniture sign behind him. I am not sure that I heard a Colt player called […]
full_text: Let me start by saying that I did not get the best look at the game. I got the Pat’s feed, so I heard too much McCourty twin banter, along with another guy who talked with a big Bob’s Discount Furniture sign behind him. I am not sure that I heard a Colt player called out by name and I am sure that I did not see a highlight of a good play by a Colt player. It was a dreadful broadcast that I eventually turned down and just accessed my roster after most plays, to see who did something good or bad. It is not likely that anyone won a job Thursday night, unless they were in pretty good shape already. If it were me, I would say that one guy lost a job and that would CB Edwards. You have to be pretty weak to be targeted during a preseason game. I’d keep Jaylon Jones in a heartbeat over him right now. One of a couple of things I liked, was seeing pass rushers from a standing position. It looked like both Curry and Gumbs were allowed to do that, so maybe they are hoping that one of them has some natural instincts that can be unleashed situationally. I thought both did a good job of not giving away an edge, but I thought they looked tentative on backside pursuit. I get that they have likely been drilled about not giving up backside contain, but it seemed weird to not see them aggressive. Another thing I liked was the screen game. Those plays had to be in response to the way D’s played us post Pittsburgh. We have been bad at that aspect for quite some time, but I think that they have figured a little something out. If they can get some good results on tape, it could slow some teams down once we get to the regular season, but more likely they will have show they can beat blitzes once the bright lights come on. As far as AR goes, it was more of the same. He looks better with his legs than with his arm. Those that want to support him should take the approach that they take with Ballard. He committed two turnovers and scored 7 points on the way to halftime deficit. If you are a bottom line type, that would not be seen as a positive. I think I would tell him that I’d like to put in some packages/gadgets for him. If he is not receptive, I’d let him know he is the 3rd string QB and that he’d remain a Colt until free agency next year. It seems like he’d be a good guy to salt games away with the running game. He would at least be relevant and seen by other teams. It is not like Leonard was good either. I do think that he could be groomed to be a good, cheap, backup for three years. I thought we showed a little better covering the middle of the field, Edwards excluded. Not perfect and not against number ones, but it still looked better than recent versions of the defense. I thought Boettcher looked active. I think Wohlers may always struggle to stay on the field, as he either has bad technique, or a death wish. I also think that we have enough pass catchers. Consider that our top six WR did not play, nor did Warren and it looked like all who were targeted, answered the bell when called upon. Hats off to Freeland for going the whole way. The O-line didn’t look like a weakness, with only Travis getting a few snap among the depth chart’s first teamers. Maybe they didn’t blow open holes, but the pocket looked clean enough to me and they evidently did a pretty good job of selling for the screens. In the grand scheme of things, not much was decided, but it was successful enough for health and six penalties for 60 yards is not cause for alarm. Mission accomplished.
